A new calculator must meet three tests: its inputs are obtainable, its calculation is reproducible, and its output helps someone take action. Rate of velocity change from initial velocity, final velocity, and time — with distance covered alongside.
Rate of velocity change from initial velocity, final velocity, and time — with the distance covered alongside.
Assumes constant acceleration. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Average acceleration a = (v₁ − v₀) ÷ t, where v₀ is the initial velocity, v₁ the final velocity, and t the time taken. With constant acceleration, the distance covered is the average velocity times time: d = ((v₀ + v₁) ÷ 2) × t. A negative result means deceleration — velocity falling rather than rising. Units must match: velocities in m/s and time in seconds give acceleration in m/s² and distance in metres.

From rest (0 m/s) to 30 m/s in 5 seconds: a = (30 − 0) ÷ 5 = 6.00 m/s². The velocity change is 30 m/s, and the distance covered is ((0 + 30) ÷ 2) × 5 = 15 × 5 = 75 m. For scale, 6 m/s² is a brisk car launch — roughly 0 to 100 km/h in about 4.6 seconds at that rate (100 km/h is 27.78 m/s, and 27.78 ÷ 6 = 4.63 s).

This page computes average acceleration over the interval, assuming it is constant. Real acceleration usually varies (an engine's pull fades as speed rises), in which case this result is the average, not the peak. It is one-dimensional: direction changes, circular motion, and vector components are not covered. Time must be above zero — an instant change (t = 0) would imply infinite acceleration, which the page refuses rather than displays.
What is the difference between velocity and acceleration?

Velocity is how fast something moves; acceleration is how fast that velocity changes. A car cruising at a steady 30 m/s has high velocity and zero acceleration; the same car speeding up from 0 to 30 m/s has positive acceleration throughout.
What does a negative acceleration mean?
Velocity is falling — braking, in everyday terms. Negative acceleration is still acceleration in the physics sense; "deceleration" is just the name for its negative case.
Because acceleration is velocity change per unit time: (m/s) ÷ s = m/s². It reads as "metres per second, per second" — each second, velocity grows by that many m/s.
How does this relate to force?
Newton's second law: force = mass × acceleration. A 1,000 kg car accelerating at 6 m/s² needs 6,000 N of net force. This page does not ask for mass, so it cannot report force.
Can I use km/h instead of m/s?
Only if you convert first: divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s, and convert time to seconds. Mixing km/h with seconds gives a number that is not m/s². The velocity calculator's conversions can help.
Yes — it is g, Earth's surface gravity. An object in free fall (ignoring air resistance) accelerates downward at about 9.81 m/s². Enter v₀ = 0, v₁ = 9.81, t = 1 to see it.

Exact age in years, months and days, total days lived, and days until the next birthday.
Your exact age in years, months and days, total days lived, and the wait until your next birthday — from calendar dates only.
Results update as you type. No calculate button. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Age = reference date − date of birth, evaluated as a calendar difference: completed years first, then completed months, then remaining days. Days lived is the plain day count between the two dates. Days until the next birthday is the day count from the reference date to the next occurrence of the birth month and day.

Born 10 May 1990, at the reference date 28 October 2026: 36 completed years (to 10 May 2026), plus 5 completed months (to 10 October 2026), plus 18 days = 36 years, 5 months, 18 days. Days lived = 13,320 days. The next birthday is 10 May 2027, which is 194 days after 28 October 2026. Set the reference date to 2026-10-28 to reproduce this result.

All dates are local calendar dates; times of day and time zones are ignored, so a birthday later today still counts as reached on its date. Leap years are handled by the calendar itself: a person born on 29 February ages by completed calendar years, and in a non-leap year this page treats 28 February as the birthday for the next-birthday count (stated here so the convention is explicit, not assumed). If the date of birth is after the reference date, no age is shown.
Is the age in years, months and days exact?
Yes, as a calendar age: completed years, then completed months, then days. It is not total days divided by 365, which would drift across leap years.
By the real calendar. The day count between two dates automatically includes 29 February in leap years, and the year/month breakdown follows calendar months of different lengths.
Age still advances by completed calendar years. For the next-birthday countdown in a non-leap year, this page uses 28 February and says so in the scope section.
No. Only calendar dates are compared, so time zones and birth times do not change the result.
What if the birth date is in the future?
No result is shown; the page asks for a birth date on or before the reference date.

Estimate the energy and CO2e of AI inference calls from your own assumptions: calls, energy per call, grid intensity, and PUE.

Estimate AI inference emissions from assumptions you enter yourself — calls, energy per call, grid carbon intensity, and facility overhead (PUE). Nothing here is a measured footprint for any specific model.

The energy-per-call and grid-intensity values are example inputs, not measured values for any model or region. Replace them with your own measured or provider-supplied figures before using the result.
Facility overhead is the difference between total energy and inference energy. If PUE is 1.0, overhead is zero.
Bars are scaled to the larger energy figure. They show how much PUE adds, not a comparison with any other system.
Each row reuses your energy-per-call, PUE, and grid inputs and varies only the call count, so the figures scale linearly.
Energy (kWh) = calls × Wh per call × PUE ÷ 1,000. Emissions (kg CO₂e) = energy × grid grams per kWh ÷ 1,000. Per-call emissions (g CO₂e) = Wh per call × PUE × grid grams per kWh ÷ 1,000.

Calls 100,000, energy 0.5 Wh per call, PUE 1.2, grid 450 gCO₂e/kWh. Energy = 100,000 × 0.5 × 1.2 ÷ 1,000 = 60 kWh. Emissions = 60 × 450 ÷ 1,000 = 27 kg CO₂e. Per call: 0.5 × 1.2 × 450 ÷ 1,000 = 0.27 g CO₂e; per 1,000 calls: 270 g CO₂e. These inputs are examples only — replace the energy-per-call and grid figures with your own before relying on the result.

This is a scenario model, not a carbon accounting result. It covers only the inference energy you describe: training, model development, hardware manufacturing, networking, cooling beyond PUE, and embodied emissions are excluded. Energy per call varies by model, hardware, batching, and prompt length, and grid intensity varies by place and time — both are user inputs here precisely because no single published value fits every case. No live emissions data or certified accounting is provided.
Energy is calls times Wh per call times PUE, divided by 1,000 to get kWh; emissions are energy times grid grams per kWh, divided by 1,000 to get kilograms of CO₂e.
Why are the carbon factor and energy per call editable?
Because they are assumptions, not constants. A different model, GPU, or region gives different values, so the page treats them as inputs you must supply and labels the defaults as examples only.

Power usage effectiveness: total facility energy divided by IT energy. A PUE of 1.2 means 20% overhead for cooling and other facility loads on top of inference energy; 1.0 means no overhead is counted.
Does this include training the model?
No. It covers only the inference calls in your scenario. Training, fine-tuning, and hardware manufacturing are separate and much larger in some cases, and are not modeled here.
Why is the result linear in call count?

Each row in the volume table reuses the same per-call figure, so doubling calls doubles the estimate. Real systems may batch or cache, which would break that linearity — another reason to replace the example per-call figure with measured data.
Can I use this for an official emissions report?

No. It is a planning estimate from your own assumptions. Formal reporting needs measured energy data, a documented grid factor for the right region and period, and the reporting framework your organisation follows.

Estimate monthly AI inference cost from your own token counts, call volume, and prices per million tokens.
Estimate monthly inference cost from token counts, call volume, and prices you enter per million tokens. Prices are your inputs, not live provider prices.
The token prices are example inputs, not live prices for any provider or model. Replace them with the prices that apply to your own account before using the result.
Monthly tokens are calls times tokens per call. Prices are applied per million tokens, as entered.
Bars are scaled to the larger cost component and show whether input or output tokens dominate the bill.
Monthly cost at different call volumes
Each row reuses your tokens per call and prices and varies only the call count, so cost scales linearly with volume.
Monthly cost = calls × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 1,000,000, with prices in USD per million tokens. Cost per call = monthly cost ÷ calls.

Input 2,500 tokens, output 800 tokens, 100,000 calls, input price $5 and output price $20 per million tokens. Input cost = 100,000 × 2,500 × 5 ÷ 1,000,000 = $1,250. Output cost = 100,000 × 800 × 20 ÷ 1,000,000 = $1,600. Total = $2,850 per month, or $0.0285 per call. The prices in this example are illustrative only — enter your own plan's prices for a usable figure.

Prices are entered per million tokens and are not live provider prices; the defaults are illustrative, not a quote for any model. Cached tokens, batch discounts, retries, failed calls, rate-limit retries, and infrastructure or staffing costs are excluded. Token counts are your averages: real calls vary, and a few long outputs can move the average materially. Taxes and currency conversion are not included.
Each call's cost is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, divided by 1,000,000; that per-call cost times the monthly call count is the monthly total.
Are the default prices real provider prices?
No. They are example inputs. Provider prices change and differ by model and tier, so enter the prices from your own plan or invoice before using the result.
Why is output cost often larger than input cost?
Output prices per token are usually higher than input prices, and long outputs add up. The breakdown table shows the split so you can see which side to optimise.
Cached or discounted tokens, batch pricing, retries, infrastructure, and staff time. If those are material for you, add them separately rather than treating this total as a full cost of ownership.
How do I estimate tokens per call?
Measure a sample of real calls: record input and output token counts, average them, and re-check after prompts change. Averages from a handful of short test calls usually understate production calls.
Does this predict my bill exactly?
No. It is an estimate from your averages and prices. Compare it with an actual invoice for one month, then adjust the token averages or prices until the model tracks reality.

Estimate the monthly net value of an AI workflow tool: time saved across a team minus the tool fee.
Estimate what an AI workflow tool is worth per month: hours saved across the team, valued at an hourly cost, minus the monthly tool fee.
Gross time value is hours saved times hourly cost. Net value subtracts the tool fee once, not per person.
Bars are scaled to the larger of gross value and fee. A fee bar taller than the gross-value bar means the tool does not pay for itself on time value alone.
Each row multiplies the monthly net value by the number of months, assuming the same usage and fee throughout. Setup or training costs are not included.
Monthly net value = people × monthly runs × minutes saved ÷ 60 × hourly cost − monthly tool fee. Hours saved = people × runs × minutes saved ÷ 60.

8 people, 20 runs each per month, 18 minutes saved per run, hourly cost $120, fee $999. Hours saved = 8 × 20 × 18 ÷ 60 = 48 hours. Gross value = 48 × $120 = $5,760. Net = $5,760 − $999 = $4,761 per month, or $595.13 per person. Over 12 months at the same usage that is $57,132, before any setup or training cost.

Time value is not automatically cash saved: valuing freed hours at full hourly cost overstates the benefit if the time is absorbed by other low-value work or idle time. Adoption rate, review and correction time, output quality, setup and training costs, and any per-seat pricing beyond the single fee input are not modeled. Minutes saved should come from timed before-and-after runs, not from vendor claims.
Hours saved are people times runs times minutes saved, divided by 60; gross value is hours times hourly cost; net value subtracts the monthly tool fee.
Is the net value cash in the bank?

Only if the freed time is redeployed to billable or otherwise valuable work. If it is absorbed elsewhere, the value is capacity gained, not cash saved — set hourly cost to the value you actually recover.
Should the fee be per person?
This page takes a single monthly fee. If your plan charges per seat, enter the total monthly fee for the whole team, or divide: enter the per-seat fee times the team size as the fee.
How do I measure minutes saved?
Time the same task with and without the tool over several real runs, including review and correction time, and use the median saving — not the best single run.
What if usage drops after the first month?
Then the monthly net falls with it. Re-run the page with the actual run count after a month of real use instead of trusting the launch-month figure.
Setup, training, integration, data-cleaning, and quality-review costs, and any change in output quality. A tool that saves time but needs heavy correction may save less than the raw minutes suggest.

Convert total growth over a holding period into a compound annual growth rate.
Start vs end, at a glance
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two values. A single growth rate hides the path: a steady climb and a volatile ride can share the same annualized figure.
Growth path at this annualized rate
The path applies the annualized rate evenly each year. It is a smoothed view, not a record of what actually happened year by year.
− 1. Total return = (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value.
Initial value $10,000 growing to $15,000 over 4 years: total gain $5,000, total return 50.00%, and annualized return (15,000 ÷ 10,000)
− 1 = 10.67%. That is the steady yearly rate that would carry $10,000 to $15,000 in 4 years.

This is a smoothed, backward-looking rate: it assumes growth compounds evenly and says nothing about volatility, fees, taxes, inflation, or cash added or withdrawn during the period. It cannot be compared directly with a simple average yearly return, and it is not a forecast.
Is annualized return the same as average yearly return?
No. A simple average of yearly returns ignores compounding. The annualized (compound) rate is the single steady rate that reproduces the total growth over the period.
What if the final value is lower than the initial value?
The result is negative, which is correct: a negative annualized rate means the value shrank at that steady yearly pace.
Can I use it for periods shorter than a year?
Yes, with years as a fraction (for example 0.5 for six months), but annualizing a short period magnifies short-term moves, so treat the result with caution.
Does it include dividends or fees?
Only if they are already reflected in the final value you enter. Dividends reinvested raise the final value; fees paid out lower it.
Why is it lower than the total return divided by years?
Because compounding does part of the work: 50% over 4 years is 10.67% compounded, not 12.50% a year, since each year's growth also earns growth in later years.
The true annual cost of a loan including fees — APR from the loan amount, nominal rate, term, and upfront fees.
The true annual cost of a loan including upfront fees — solved from the monthly payment, not approximated.
Monthly payments, no early repayment. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.
First the monthly payment at the nominal rate: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)

), where P is the loan amount, i is the monthly nominal rate, and n is the number of payments. APR is then the monthly rate r that makes the present value of those payments equal the amount actually received (P − fees): (P − fees) = PMT × (1 − (1 + r)
) ÷ r. The nominal APR is 12 × r; the effective APR is (1 + r)
− 1. The page solves for r by bisection, not by an approximation formula.
$10,000 at a 6% nominal rate over 36 months with $300 of upfront fees: the monthly payment is 10,000 × 0.005 ÷ (1 − 1.005

) = $304.22, and $304.22 × 36 = $10,951.90 is repaid in total. The borrower actually receives 10,000 − 300 = $9,700, and the monthly rate that discounts 36 payments of $304.22 back to $9,700 is 0.6714%, so the nominal APR is 12 × 0.6714% = 8.06% (8.36% effective). The $300 fee lifts the true cost from 6% to 8.06% — that gap is exactly what APR exists to reveal.

This page assumes fixed monthly payments, a fixed nominal rate, and a single upfront fee deducted from the amount received. It does not model variable rates, balloon payments, early-repayment penalties, ongoing monthly charges, or fees paid separately rather than deducted — each of those changes the APR. Lenders' disclosed APRs follow jurisdiction-specific rules about which charges count; this page's figure is a transparent calculation from the four inputs shown, not a lender disclosure. If fees are zero, APR equals the nominal rate (effective APR is slightly higher because of monthly compounding).
Why is APR higher than the interest rate?

Because APR spreads the fees across the loan as well as the interest. In the example, $300 of fees on a $10,000 loan lifts the cost from 6% to 8.06%. A loan with a lower rate but heavy fees can easily cost more than a higher-rate loan with no fees.
What is the difference between nominal and effective APR?
Nominal APR is 12 times the monthly rate (8.06% here). Effective APR compounds that monthly rate over a year ((1 + r)
− 1 = 8.36%). Lenders usually quote the nominal figure; the effective figure is what compounding actually costs.
Do I compare APRs or monthly payments?

Compare APRs for loans of the same term and structure — it is the only figure that includes fees. Monthly payments alone hide fees, and a longer term can look cheaper per month while costing far more overall.
What if the loan has no fees?

Then the amount received equals the loan amount, the solving rate equals the nominal monthly rate, and nominal APR equals the nominal rate. The effective APR is still slightly higher because interest compounds monthly.
Does a shorter term raise or lower APR?
With the same fees, a shorter term raises APR: the same $300 is spread over fewer payments, so each payment carries more fee cost. That is why small short loans often show startling APRs.
Is this the same APR my lender quotes?

It should be close if the inputs match and the lender counts the same charges. If it differs, check which fees the lender included or excluded, and whether the rate is fixed — a variable rate makes any single APR figure an estimate.

Convert area between square metres, square feet, acres, and mu — type a value and see all four units at once.
All four units describe the same area; the mu figure uses the definition in the formula table below.
Convert the source value to square metres, then divide by the target unit's square-metre factor:

The square-foot and acre factors are exact international definitions. The mu factor 666.6667 m² is the commonly used Chinese definition (1 mu = 2000/3 m², rounded here); cadastral and local land units may follow other definitions.

100 m² ÷ 0.09290304 m²/ft² = 1,076.391042 ft². The same 100 m² is 100 ÷ 4,046.8564224 = 0.024711 acre, and 100 ÷ 666.6667 = 0.150000 mu (shown as 0.15 after display rounding; the unrounded value is 0.14999999 because the mu factor itself is rounded).

Negative areas are rejected as invalid. Display values are rounded to 6 decimal places; the underlying calculation is not rounded. The mu definition varies by place and era, so for legal or cadastral use confirm the definition your authority applies — this page uses 666.6667 m² per mu throughout.
A Chinese area unit. This page uses the common modern definition 1 mu = 666.6667 m² (2000/3 m²). Older or local definitions differ, so check before using it for land documents.
How many square feet are in a square metre?
1 m² = 10.76391041671 ft², because 1 ft² = 0.09290304 m² exactly.
One acre = 4,046.8564224 m², about 0.4047 hectares. An American football field (without end zones) is about 0.756 acre.
Why does the mu result show 0.15 instead of 0.14999999?
Display rounding to 6 decimal places. The full-precision value is kept for the reverse conversion shown in the chips.
Not on this page: the four units here are the ones the original tool offered. Convert hectares to square metres first (1 ha = 10,000 m²) and enter that value.

Score a task for automation fit from rule clarity, digitisation, volume, and risk — with every scoring rule shown.
Score a task for automation fit from rule clarity, digitisation, volume, and risk. Every point comes from a stated rule below — this is a transparent checklist, not a validated predictor.
Component points are shown before clamping. The final score is the raw total clamped to the 0–100 range.
Bars are scaled to 40 points so components can be compared; volume is capped at 30 points, so its bar can never reach the top of this scale.
Each row changes one input from your scenario and holds the others fixed, so you can see which improvement matters most. These are hypothetical scores, not predictions.
Score = clamp(4 × rule clarity + 3 × digitisation + min(30, frequency × minutes ÷ 600 × 3) − 2 × risk, 0, 100). All three ratings are on a 0–10 scale and are clamped to that range before scoring.
Frequency × minutes ÷ 600 × 3, capped at 30 — 600 minutes (10 hours) per month earns 3 points, so 100 hours earns the cap
Bands used by the verdict: 70–100 strong candidate, 40–69 review first, below 40 weak fit. The bands are this page's own reading of the score, not a validated threshold.

Frequency 80 runs per month, 15 minutes per run, rule clarity 8, digitisation 7, risk 4. Rule points = 4 × 8 = 32. Digitisation points = 3 × 7 = 21. Volume = 80 × 15 ÷ 600 × 3 = 6, below the 30 cap. Risk deduction = 2 × 4 = 8. Total = 32 + 21 + 6 − 8 = 51 out of 100 — a mixed case in the 40–69 review band. Monthly time on the task is 80 × 15 = 1,200 minutes (20 hours). Note: the source page labelled this result in minutes; the unit is points out of 100, and this page corrects that label.

This is a custom weighted checklist, not a validated scientific score and not a prediction of automation success. The weights (4, 3, volume cap 30, risk 2) and the 70/40 bands are heuristic choices made for this page; changing them changes the score. It does not assess implementation cost, exception rates, data quality, change management, or regulatory constraints — a high score still needs a pilot, and a low score may still be worth automating for compliance or coverage reasons.

Rule clarity times 4, plus digitisation times 3, plus volume points (frequency times minutes divided by 600, times 3, capped at 30), minus risk times 2, with the total clamped between 0 and 100. The full rule table is in the Formula section.
70–100 is read as a strong candidate, 40–69 as review first, below 40 as weak fit. These are this page's own bands for reading the score, not externally validated thresholds.
So sheer volume cannot outweigh unclear rules or undigitised inputs. A task run constantly but governed by judgement calls should not outscore a clear, digitised, lower-volume task by volume alone.
Why does risk subtract only up to 20 points?

Because risk is one factor among four, not a veto. A high-risk task can still score in the review band if everything else is strong — but that is exactly when a human-in-the-loop design, rather than full automation, should be considered.
How should I rate rule clarity and digitisation honestly?

Rule clarity 10 means the decision steps are written down and two people would reach the same outcome; digitisation 10 means inputs and outputs are already structured data. If either needs judgement or paper handling, rate it lower and note why.
Does a high score guarantee savings?
No. It says the task looks automatable, not that the project will pay off. Cost, exception handling, and maintenance still need their own estimate before committing.

Blood pressure category from systolic and diastolic readings, using the standard adult bands, with pulse pressure shown alongside.
Which standard adult band a reading falls in — plus pulse pressure. This is information only, not a diagnosis.
Enter one reading in mmHg. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

A reading takes the higher of the two bands it qualifies for: 135/85 is Stage 1 because the diastolic 85 falls in the Stage 1 range even though the systolic 135 is also Stage 1. Bands follow the widely used adult classification; children, pregnancy, and some conditions use different thresholds.

Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. Category is assigned from the higher of the systolic band and the diastolic band, with readings over 180 systolic or over 120 diastolic flagged as hypertensive crisis regardless of the other number.

135/85: systolic 135 falls in 130–139 (Stage 1) and diastolic 85 falls in 80–89 (Stage 1), so the category is Stage 1 hypertension. Pulse pressure = 135 − 85 = 50 mmHg. A single reading does not diagnose hypertension — diagnosis rests on repeated readings over time, interpreted by a clinician.

One reading is a snapshot: blood pressure varies through the day, with stress, caffeine, exercise, and cuff position. This page does not diagnose, stage, or recommend treatment for any condition, and it does not replace a clinician's reading of your history. If you get a crisis-range reading, especially with chest pain, shortness of breath, or neurological symptoms, seek emergency care promptly rather than re-measuring repeatedly. Thresholds here are the standard adult bands; they do not apply to children or to pregnancy without clinical adjustment.
What do the two numbers mean?
Systolic is the pressure when the heart contracts; diastolic is the pressure between beats. Both matter — the category uses whichever falls in the higher band.
Does one high reading mean I have hypertension?
No. Diagnosis requires repeated elevated readings over time, usually including readings taken outside the clinic. A single high reading is a reason to recheck, not a diagnosis.
Why is my clinic reading higher than at home?
White-coat effect: stress in a clinical setting raises readings for many people. Home readings taken with correct technique are often lower and are part of the diagnostic picture.
How should I measure for a fair reading?

Seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart height, correct cuff size, no caffeine or exercise in the prior 30 minutes, and a few minutes of rest first. Two readings a minute apart, averaged, beat one rushed reading.
The gap between systolic and diastolic — 50 mmHg in the example. A wide gap can reflect stiff arteries, but it is interpreted alongside the absolute numbers, not alone.
When should I seek urgent care?

For a reading over 180 systolic or over 120 diastolic, especially with chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, vision changes, or difficulty speaking — seek emergency care promptly.

Body mass index from height and weight — the standard adult categories, BMI Prime, and the healthy-weight range for your height.
Standard adult cut-offs: underweight below 18.5, healthy weight 18.5–24.9, overweight 25.0–29.9, obesity 30.0 and above. The bar is scaled to 40 so higher values stay visible.
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²). BMI Prime = BMI ÷ 25. Ponderal Index = weight (kg) ÷ height³ (m³). The healthy-weight range is the weight range that gives a BMI of 18.5–24.9 at your height.

BMI is a screening measure for adults, not a diagnosis and not a direct measure of body fat. It does not distinguish muscle from fat, so it can misclassify very muscular or very slight builds, and it does not apply in the same way to children, whose categories use age- and sex-specific percentiles. Height and weight are taken as entered; no other personal circumstances are modelled.
What do the adult categories mean?

Underweight is below 18.5, healthy weight is 18.5–24.9, overweight is 25.0–29.9, and obesity is 30.0 and above. These are the standard interval definitions, used here only as labels for the computed number.
Does a BMI outside the healthy range mean something is wrong?
No — not by itself. BMI is a screening number, not a diagnosis. It says nothing about body composition, fitness, or health on its own.
BMI divided by 25, the top of the healthy range. A value of 1.00 sits exactly at that boundary; 0.95 is 5% below it.
Why does the metric equivalent differ slightly from my entry?
Converting feet/inches/pounds to centimetres/kilograms rounds to one decimal place. The underlying calculation uses the full converted values, so display rounding does not change the result.
No. This calculation runs locally in your browser and the values you enter are not sent to a CalcMintly database.
Can I use this for a child?
No. Children's BMI is interpreted against age- and sex-specific growth percentiles, which this page does not model.

Bars are scaled to the larger of the two values. The only difference between the two bars is the sex constant (+5 for male, −161 for female) in the Mifflin–St Jeor equation.
BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age (years) + 5 for men or − 161 for women. This is the Mifflin–St Jeor equation.
. That is 9,811 kcal per week and 42,045 kcal per 30 days. With the male constant (+5 instead of −161) the same inputs give 1,567.5 kcal/day. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

BMR is resting expenditure only — it excludes activity, digestion, and exercise, so it is lower than total daily expenditure. The Mifflin–St Jeor equation is a population estimate: it was fitted to group averages, so individual results vary with body composition, illness, medications, and other factors the inputs do not capture. It is not a metabolic test and not a personal energy prescription.
The energy the body uses at complete rest to maintain basic functions. Any activity on top of rest adds to it, which is why total daily expenditure is higher.
Why do men and women get different results?

The Mifflin–St Jeor equation adds +5 for men and subtracts 161 for women, reflecting average differences in the populations the equation was fitted to. It is a group adjustment, not a measurement of any individual.
Is BMR the same as the calories I need each day?
No. Daily need also includes activity. Multiply BMR by an activity factor — or use the TDEE Calculator — for a total daily estimate.
It is an estimate from a population equation. Individual values can differ materially; only a metabolic test measures resting expenditure directly.
Yes, through the −5 × age term: each additional year lowers the estimate by 5 kcal/day at fixed weight and height.

. Implied fat mass is 65 × 0.285 = 18.5 kg and implied lean mass is 46.5 kg. With the male sex term the same inputs give 17.7%. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

This is not a direct body-composition measurement: no skinfold, scan, or weighing method is involved, and the equation only recombines BMI, age, and sex. It can be inaccurate for athletes, older adults, and many body types, because two people with the same BMI and age can carry very different amounts of muscle and fat. The fat-mass and lean-mass figures are just the percentage applied to the entered weight, not separately measured quantities.
Is this the same as a body-fat scan?
No. A scan or skinfold test measures the body directly; this page only applies a population equation to BMI, age, and sex.
Why does the result change with sex?
The equation subtracts 10.8 points for men, reflecting average differences in the population it was fitted to. It is a group adjustment, not a measurement of the individual.
Why can it be wrong for athletes?
Because BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. A muscular person can have a high BMI — and therefore a high estimated body fat — while carrying little fat.
What do fat mass and lean mass mean here?
They are the estimated percentage applied to your entered weight (fat mass = weight × percentage; lean mass = the rest). They are not separately measured.
Does the estimate work for children?
No. The equation is an adult population formula and is not validated for children.

Find the units and revenue needed for contribution margin to cover fixed costs.
Find the units — and the revenue — needed for contribution margin to cover fixed costs.
Every unit sold beyond break-even adds one unit of contribution margin to profit, at these prices and costs.
At break-even the two bars are equal by definition: total contribution exactly covers fixed costs.
Fixed costs and variable cost are held at the values above; only the price changes across rows.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (unit price − unit variable cost). Break-even revenue = break-even units × unit price. Contribution margin per unit = unit price − unit variable cost.

Fixed costs $50,000, price $200, variable cost $120: contribution margin is $200 − $120 = $80 per unit, so break-even units = $50,000 ÷ $80 = 625 units, and break-even revenue = 625 × $200 = $125,000.

Price must exceed variable cost, or break-even never arrives. Product mix, taxes, stepped costs that jump at capacity limits, volume discounts, and changing prices are excluded — this is a single-product, constant-price model.
How does the break even calculator work?
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (unit price − unit variable cost). It finds the sales volume where total contribution exactly pays the fixed costs.
What if the price is below the variable cost?
Then every sale loses money and there is no break-even volume — selling more only deepens the loss. The price must cover the variable cost before fixed costs can be recovered.
Price minus variable cost per unit: the amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs and then profit. Here it is $80 per unit at the example values.
Does selling past break-even mean pure profit?
At these assumptions, yes for each extra unit — but only until stepped costs, capacity limits, or price cuts change the picture. Real businesses rarely hold all three inputs constant.
No. Treat the break-even revenue as pre-tax revenue and apply your own tax treatment separately.
No. With a product mix you need a weighted-average contribution margin. This calculator models one product at one price.

Why is this only an estimate?

Area, circumference, and diameter of a circle from its radius, with the formulas shown and worked through.
Area, circumference, and diameter of a circle from its radius — in whatever unit you enter, out in the same unit.
Enter the radius in any unit — metres, centimetres, inches — and the results come back in that unit (square units for area). Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.
Area = π × radius². Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Diameter = 2 × radius. π is used at full precision and results are rounded to two decimals for display.
Radius 5: area = π × 5² = π × 25 = 78.54. Circumference = 2 × π × 5 = 31.42. Diameter = 10. If the radius was 5 cm, the area is 78.54 cm² and the circumference is 31.42 cm.

This is a perfect circle: one radius, one centre. Ellipses, arcs, sectors, and rings need their own formulas and are not covered here. The page does not convert units — a radius in inches gives an area in square inches; convert first if you need another unit.
Radius or diameter — which do I enter?
Radius: the distance from the centre to the edge. If you only know the diameter (edge to edge through the centre), halve it first — or read the diameter chip above in reverse.
Why is area in square units?
Because area covers a surface. A radius of 5 cm gives 78.54 cm², not 78.54 cm. Mixing the two is the most common circle mistake.
What value of pi is used?
Full double-precision pi (3.141592653589793…), not 3.14. The difference only matters past the second decimal, but there is no reason to round early.
How does area grow with radius?
With the square: doubling the radius quadruples the area. A radius-10 circle has area 314.16, exactly four times the radius-5 area of 78.54.
Can I use this for a sphere?
No. A sphere's surface area is 4πr² and its volume is (4/3)πr³ — different formulas for a 3D object.
What if I know the circumference instead?
Divide it by 2π to get the radius, then enter that here. For a circumference of 31.42, the radius is 31.42 ÷ 6.2832 = 5.

End of the month, matching the source calculator's convention. Start-of-month contributions would earn one extra month of interest each and give a slightly higher total.

Bars are scaled to the larger of the two volumes. The waste slice is the extra you order on top of the exact rectangular volume.
Order volume at different waste allowances
Same length, width and depth; only the waste allowance changes. Use this to see how sensitive the order is to the allowance you pick.
Net volume = length × width × depth. Waste volume = net volume × waste rate. Order volume = net volume × (1 + waste rate).

Length 10 m, width 4 m, depth 0.15 m: net volume = 10 × 4 × 0.15 = 6 m³. At an 8% waste allowance, waste volume = 6.00 × 0.08 = 0.48 m³, so order volume = 6.48 m³ (228.84 ft³). These are the example defaults above; replace them with your own measurements.

This covers a single rectangular pour only. Subgrade variation, reinforcement displacement, irregular shapes, sloped sections, supplier minimum loads and rounding to the supplier's ordering unit can all change the order. No price is calculated: enter no price here, so compare supplier quotes against the order volume yourself.
Why add a waste allowance at all?
Because a real pour rarely matches the exact rectangular volume: spillage, uneven subgrade and formwork gaps all consume extra concrete. The allowance is your buffer, not a supplier charge.
What if my shape is not a rectangle?

Split it into measured rectangles, calculate each one, and add the net volumes before applying waste. Do not force an irregular shape into one rectangle and hope the waste allowance absorbs the difference.
Measure the finished slab thickness at several points and use a representative value. If depth varies a lot, split the pour into zones with different depths instead of averaging blindly.
Does this include the supplier's minimum load?
No. If your order is below a supplier minimum, the supplier may still charge for the minimum. Check that before ordering, especially for small pours.
Can I convert the result to cubic feet or litres?
Yes: 1 m³ = 35.3147 ft³ = 1,000 litres. The breakdown table shows the order in all three units.
Does this tell me what the concrete will cost?
No, there is no price input on this page. Multiply the order volume by your supplier's quoted price per unit yourself; prices vary by mix, location and delivery terms.

Estimate the ROI of a piece of creator content from production cost, views, conversion, order value, and margin.
Estimate a piece of content's return: production cost against the profit from the orders its views are assumed to generate.
Revenue is orders times order value; gross profit applies the margin to revenue. ROI is net profit divided by production cost.
Bars are scaled to the larger of production cost and gross profit. Profit must clear the cost bar to be positive.
Each row reuses your conversion rate, order value, margin, and cost and varies only views, so you can find the view count that breaks even.
ROI = (views × conversion% × order value × margin% − production cost) ÷ production cost × 100%. Orders = views × conversion%. Gross profit = orders × order value × margin%.

Cost $1,800, views 50,000, conversion 0.8%, order value $199, margin 55%. Orders = 50,000 × 0.8% = 400. Revenue = 400 × $199 = $79,600. Gross profit = $79,600 × 55% = $43,780. Net = $43,780 − $1,800 = $41,980. ROI = $41,980 ÷ $1,800 × 100% = 2,332.22%. Break-even views at these rates are about 2,056 views (cost divided by profit per view of $0.8756: 0.8% x $199 x 55%).

Views and conversion are your assumptions, not a traffic forecast; a view count does not guarantee that conversion rate, and past content is only a rough guide. Revenue alone is not profit — the margin input is doing that work, so an overstated margin overstates ROI directly. Attribution is not modeled: orders credited to the piece may have been influenced by other channels, and production cost here is a single figure, excluding distribution, promotion, and revision costs unless you include them in it.
Orders are views times the conversion rate; gross profit is orders times order value times margin; ROI is gross profit minus production cost, divided by production cost, times 100%.
What conversion rate should I use?
A measured one from comparable past content with the same offer and audience, not a platform average. If you have no measured rate, run the page at several rates and see how far ROI moves.
Why is margin in the formula?
Because revenue is not profit. Without margin, a high-revenue, low-margin product looks far better than it is. Enter the gross margin on the orders themselves, after product and fulfilment costs.

Everything spent making the piece: creator time or fees, editing, props, locations, and licences. Add paid promotion separately if you want it counted — either include it in the cost or run a second scenario.

Arithmetically yes, when a low-cost piece converts well, as in the worked example. That is a property of the ratio, not evidence the next piece will repeat it — small costs make the percentage swing wildly.
No. Views are an input you supply. The page tells you what a given view count would be worth at your conversion and margin, not how many views you will get.

Estimate payoff time and interest when making a fixed monthly card payment.
Bars are scaled to the total paid. At card rates the interest slice is large even for a moderate balance, which is why raising the payment helps so much.
Interest each month is opening balance times APR divided by 12; the payment then reduces the balance. The final payment is capped at what remains.
Each month: interest = opening balance × APR ÷ 12; ending balance = opening balance + interest − payment. The simulation repeats until the balance reaches zero.
Balance $10,000 at 18% APR with $300 a month: the first month's interest is $150.00, and the card pays off in 47 months with $3,967.21 of interest, for $13,967.21 total.

Fixed APR, fixed monthly payment, no new purchases, no fees, no penalty rates, and no minimum-payment rules. Real cards vary the APR, charge fees, and often set the minimum as a percentage of the balance, so this is a fixed-payment estimate, not a card statement forecast.
What if my payment is less than the monthly interest?
The balance grows and the card never pays off at that payment. The calculator flags this: raise the payment above the first month's interest figure.
Why is the interest so high compared with a loan?
Because the APR is high and the balance falls slowly at first. Most of the early payments cover interest, not principal.
Does paying more than the minimum help?
Yes, disproportionately: a higher payment both cuts the balance faster and shortens the period over which interest accrues.
Not included. New purchases add to the balance and extend the payoff time; this calculator assumes none.
Is the APR the same as the interest rate?
APR is the yearly rate used here, including the card's stated rate. Fees are separate and are not modeled.
Convert an amount at a rate you enter, less an optional fee — no market rate is fetched or implied.
Convert an amount at a rate you type in, less a fee percentage — this page never pretends to know the market rate.
Exchange rate (example — replace with the actual rate)
The fee is taken from the converted amount. Enter the rate your provider actually quotes, not a rate from memory.
Amount received = source amount × exchange rate × (1 − fee rate). Equivalently: gross = amount × rate; fee amount = gross × fee %; received = gross − fee amount.
No rate is fetched from any market source. The default 7.2 is an example placeholder carried over from the original tool, labelled as such — it is not a quote, not current, and not a recommendation.
1,000 × 7.2 = 7,200 gross. A 1% fee is 7,200 × 0.01 = 72, so the amount received is 7,200 − 72 = 7,128. The effective rate is 7,128 ÷ 1,000 = 7.128 per unit.

This page does not provide a live or market exchange rate, and the default rate is an example only. Banks and payment providers add spreads and fixed fees that this single fee percentage may not capture; confirm the actual rate, spread, and any fixed charge before sending money. Display values are rounded to 6 decimal places; real providers round to the currency's smallest unit, which can change the final cents.
Is the default rate the current market rate?
No. It is an example value (7.2) carried over from the original tool, clearly labelled as an example. This page fetches no market data — always replace it with a rate your provider quotes.
Does the fee cover the provider's spread?
Only if you fold the spread into the fee percentage yourself. A provider quoting a worse rate than the market is charging you a hidden spread on top of any stated fee.
What if the fee is a fixed amount, not a percentage?
Subtract it from the gross yourself: received = amount × rate − fixed fee. This page models percentage fees only.
Why is the amount received lower than amount × rate?
Because the fee percentage is deducted from the converted amount. With a 0% fee the two are equal.
Can I convert in the other direction?
Yes: divide instead of multiplying. If 1,000 units buy 7,128 at the example rate and fee, the reverse effective rate is 1,000 ÷ 7,128 = 0.140292 per unit.

Why does my 1 TB drive show less than 1 TB?
Partly this base difference: 10^12 bytes = 931.32 GiB at base 1024. Filesystem overhead accounts for the rest.
How many MB in a GB?
1,024 MB at base 1024, or 1,000 MB at base 1000 — the answer depends on the base, so always state it.
No — bytes only. 1 byte = 8 bits; convert bits to bytes first (divide by 8) and enter that value.

Your debt-to-income ratio from gross monthly income and monthly debt payments, with the housing ratio and the bands lenders commonly use.
Monthly debt payments as a share of gross monthly income — the back-end DTI lenders look at, plus the housing-only front-end ratio.
Other debts means credit cards, student loans, personal loans, and any other required monthly payments. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

DTI = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income × 100. Housing ratio = housing payment ÷ gross monthly income × 100. Income here is gross (before tax), because that is the figure lenders use.

Income $6,000 a month, housing $1,500, auto $300, other debts $200: total debts are $2,000, so DTI = $2,000 ÷ $6,000 = 33.33%. The housing ratio alone is $1,500 ÷ $6,000 = 25.00%. Both sit in the range lenders commonly describe as manageable (at or under 36% for total DTI).

The bands below are common lender guidelines, not rules: individual lenders weigh credit history, savings, and loan type alongside DTI, and some loan programs allow higher ratios. Only required minimum payments count — paying extra voluntarily does not raise your DTI, and everyday spending (food, utilities, subscriptions) is not debt and is not included. Self-employed income is harder to document; lenders often use an average of recent tax years rather than one good month.
What counts as a debt payment?

Required minimum payments: mortgage or rent, auto loans, student loans, personal loans, and credit card minimums. Child support and alimony count where they apply. Groceries, utilities, and subscriptions do not.
What is the difference between front-end and back-end DTI?
Front-end is housing only (25.00% in the example); back-end is all debts (33.33%). Lenders usually care most about back-end, but some also cap front-end, often around 28%.
No. Many lenders prefer 36% or under, some accept up to 43%, and certain programs go higher with compensating factors. Treat the bands as guidance, not approval odds.
Should I use gross or take-home pay?
Gross, before tax. Using take-home pay would overstate the ratio and mismatch how lenders compute it.
How do I lower my DTI?

Pay down a small debt entirely (removing its payment helps more than trimming a large balance), avoid new monthly obligations before applying, and report all stable income — a side income with a paper trail counts.
Does paying extra on a loan help my DTI?
Not until the loan is gone. DTI uses the required minimum payment, so extra payments only help once the debt is fully paid off and its payment disappears.

Estimate the annual cost of digital clutter: monthly storage fees plus the value of time spent searching for things, and how fast a cleanup could pay for itself.
Bars are scaled to the larger component. Search time is an opportunity cost valued at your hourly figure, not cash you pay out.
Annual cost at different weekly search minutes
Same storage fee and hourly value; only the weekly search minutes change.
Annual value = monthly storage fee × 12 + weekly search minutes ÷ 60 × 52 × hourly value. Monthly average = annual value ÷ 12. Cleanup payback = cleanup hours × hourly value ÷ monthly average.

Monthly storage 68, 45 search minutes per week, hourly value 80, cleanup 6 hours: storage = 68 × 12 = 816.00; search time = 45 ÷ 60 × 52 = 39 hours per year, valued at 39 × 80 = 3,120.00; annual cost = 816.00 + 3,120.00 = 3,936.00. Cleanup value = 6 × 80 = 480.00; monthly average = 3,936.00 ÷ 12 = 328.00; payback = 480.00 ÷ 328.00 = 1.46 months. These are example inputs — your hourly value is a judgement, not a market rate.

Search time is an opportunity cost, and the model does not prove cleanup will eliminate it: a cleanup may reduce search time without removing it, and the payback figure assumes the full monthly average is recovered. Storage fees are cash costs; search-time value is not cash unless the freed time is actually used productively. Your hourly value should reflect what your time is worth to you, not a wage claim.
Annual value = monthly storage fee × 12 + weekly search minutes ÷ 60 × 52 × hourly value. Cleanup payback divides cleanup time value by the monthly average.
Is the search-time figure real money?

= 2.1566. At 2% the factor over 26 years is 1.67; at 5% it is 3.56. Small rate differences compound into large ones.
Is the average rate the same as actual CPI?

Only if you enter the true average. Year-by-year CPI in most economies has ranged from near zero to double digits, so a flat 3% is a simplification. Use it for intuition and what-if comparisons; use a CPI table for historical claims.
It means $100 today buys roughly what $46.37 bought in 2000. It does not mean anyone held $46.37 — it is the same purchasing power expressed in the older year's prices.
How is this different from the present value calculator?
The maths is identical — both use (1 + r)
— but the rate means something different. Present value discounts by a return or cost of capital; inflation adjustment rescales by price levels. Same formula, different question.
Yes — deflation. A negative rate shrinks the growth factor below 1, so past money is worth less today than it was then. Enter a negative rate to model a deflationary period.
Why do old salaries sound so small?

Because of exactly this factor. A $30,000 salary in 2000 equals about $64,700 in 2026 dollars at 3% average inflation (30,000 × 2.1566). Comparing nominal amounts across decades without adjusting misleads in both directions.

Estimate how many months of expected extra income it takes to repay tuition plus the value of study time.
Estimate the payback time for learning: tuition plus the value of your study hours, repaid by the expected monthly income gain.
Expected monthly gain already includes the probability adjustment: a $2,500 gain at 60% counts as $1,500 per month.
Bars compare the full investment with the expected gain over the first 12 months. If the gain bar is shorter, payback runs beyond a year.
Each row is expected cumulative gain minus the full investment, assuming the monthly gain starts immediately and stays constant. A delayed start pushes every row later.

Payback months = (tuition + learning hours × hourly value) ÷ (expected monthly raise × probability%). Expected monthly benefit = expected monthly raise × probability%. Net after N months = expected monthly benefit × N − total investment.

Tuition $12,000, 160 hours at $60, expected monthly gain $2,500 at 60% probability. Total investment = $12,000 + 160 × $60 = $21,600. Expected monthly benefit = $2,500 × 60% = $1,500. Payback = $21,600 ÷ $1,500 = 14.4 months. Net after 12 months = $1,500 × 12 − $21,600 = −$3,600; after 24 months = $1,500 × 24 − $21,600 = $14,400.

Expected income and probability are assumptions, not measured outcomes: a course provider's placement figure is not your probability. A zero expected monthly benefit has no finite financial payback, and the model assumes the gain starts immediately and never changes — real gains are delayed, partial, and may fade. Non-financial benefits (enjoyment, mobility, option value) are real but are not counted here, and neither are taxes on extra income, exam or material fees beyond the tuition input, or the risk of not completing the course.
Total investment (tuition plus study hours times hourly value) divided by the expected monthly benefit, which is the expected monthly raise times its probability.
Why include the value of study time?
Because hours spent learning have an opportunity cost. Ignoring them flatters expensive, time-heavy courses; valuing them at your hourly rate keeps the comparison honest.

Your honest estimate that you achieve the stated gain, given your background and the local market — not a provider's headline rate. Run the page at half your first guess to see how sensitive payback is.
What if the gain starts months later?
Add those months to the payback figure. The model assumes income starts at once; a six-month job search turns a 14.4-month payback into roughly 20.4 months from enrolment.

No. Satisfaction, career mobility, and the option to change fields are excluded. A course can fail this financial test and still be worth doing — but that should be a conscious choice, not an accident of the maths.
Why is there no payback when the gain is zero?
Because dividing by zero has no finite answer. If the expected gain is genuinely zero, the investment is never repaid by income, whatever its other merits.

Solve ax + b = 0 for x, and read slope, intercepts, and the graph of a line in slope-intercept form.
Solve ax + b = 0 for x — plus the slope, intercepts, and equation of a line in slope-intercept form.
Line slope m (for y = mx + c)
Line intercept c (for y = mx + c)
Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

For ax + b = 0 with a ≠ 0: x = −b ÷ a. For a line in slope-intercept form y = mx + c: the slope is m (rise over run), the y-intercept is c (the value at x = 0), and the x-intercept is −c ÷ m (the x value where y = 0, when m ≠ 0). If a = 0, the equation ax + b = 0 has no solution unless b is also 0, in which case every x is a solution.

3x + 6 = 0: x = −6 ÷ 3 = −2. Check: 3 × (−2) + 6 = 0. For the line y = 2x + 3: the slope is 2 (y rises 2 for each 1 step in x), the y-intercept is 3, and the x-intercept is −3 ÷ 2 = −1.50. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3) and the x-axis at (−1.50, 0).

This page solves single linear equations in one variable and describes straight lines. It does not solve quadratics (see the quadratic equation calculator), systems of equations (see the system of equations calculator), or inequalities — though the x-intercept of y = mx + c does tell you where the sign of mx + c changes. Inputs are plain numbers; fractions must be entered as decimals, and very large or tiny coefficients may lose precision in display, though the underlying arithmetic is standard double precision.

Then the equation is b = 0, which does not involve x. If b is also 0, every value of x satisfies it (the equation is an identity). If b is not 0, no value of x satisfies it. The page says which case applies instead of dividing by zero.
What does the slope actually mean?
Rise over run: how much y changes when x increases by 1. A slope of 2 means y climbs 2 per x step; a slope of −0.5 means y falls half a unit per x step. A slope of 0 is a horizontal line.
How do I read the x-intercept?

It is where the line crosses the x-axis, i.e. where y = 0. For y = 2x + 3, solving 2x + 3 = 0 gives x = −1.50 — the same calculation as the equation solver, which is no coincidence: intercepts are just solutions of the equation.
Enter them as decimals (1/2 as 0.5). The page shows results to two decimals; repeating decimals such as 1/3 display as 0.33, so for exact fractional work keep the fraction form alongside.
What is the difference between slope-intercept and standard form?

Slope-intercept form y = mx + c exposes the slope and y-intercept directly. Standard form Ax + By = C is the same line rearranged: m = −A ÷ B and c = C ÷ B (when B ≠ 0). This page works in slope-intercept form.
Substituting the solution back catches sign errors, the most common mistake in linear equations. For 3x + 6 = 0, x = −2 checks out because 3(−2) + 6 = 0; x = 2 would give 12, not 0.
Bars are scaled to the total scheduled payment. Early payments are mostly interest; the principal share grows as the balance falls.
Amortization uses the scheduled payment only; extra payments are reflected in the payoff figures above, not in this table.
Monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12. Monthly payment = principal × monthly rate × (1 + monthly rate)
− 1]. Total interest = payment × payments − principal. With a 0% rate the payment is principal ÷ payments.

Principal $300,000 at 6.5% for 30 years (360 payments): monthly payment $1,896.20, total interest $382,633.47, total paid $682,633.47. In the first year $19,401.27 goes to interest and $3,353.18 to principal, leaving $296,646.82.

Fixed rate, no fees, no taxes or insurance, and payments made on time every month. Variable rates, balloon payments, prepayment penalties, and payment holidays are not modeled. Extra payments are applied to principal in the month they are paid.
Why is the first-year interest so high?
Interest is charged on the full balance, so early payments are mostly interest. As the balance falls, the same payment covers more principal.
Do extra payments really save that much?
Yes, because every extra dollar cuts the balance that future interest is charged on. The saving compounds over the remaining term.
The payment is simply principal divided by the number of payments, and total interest is $0.
Is this the same as a mortgage payment?
Only the principal-and-interest part. A mortgage bill usually adds tax, insurance, and possibly PMI and HOA, which the mortgage calculator covers.
What if I miss a payment?
Not modeled here. Missed or late payments typically add fees and interest and extend the payoff date.

Selling price from cost and markup percent, with profit per unit and the equivalent margin — and the markup-versus-margin distinction explained.
Selling price from cost and markup percent — plus profit per unit and the equivalent margin, so markup and margin are never confused again.

Selling price = cost × (1 + markup ÷ 100). Profit per unit = selling price − cost. Margin = profit ÷ selling price × 100 — note the denominator is the price, not the cost, which is why margin and markup are different numbers for the same product.

Cost $40 with a 50% markup: selling price = $40 × 1.50 = $60.00. Profit per unit = $60.00 − $40 = $20.00. Equivalent margin = $20.00 ÷ $60.00 = 33.33%. The same product is "50% markup" and "33.33% margin" at once — both correct, measured against different bases.

Cost here means unit cost (materials, production, or purchase price). It does not include overheads, shipping, payment fees, or tax unless you fold them into the cost input. The page prices one unit; multiply by quantity for a batch. A markup below 0% would mean selling under cost — the page requires zero or above, since pricing under cost is a deliberate loss-leader decision, not a markup calculation.
Markup or margin — which should I use?
Markup for setting prices from cost (the usual shop-floor question); margin for reporting profitability (profit as a share of revenue). Convert with margin = markup ÷ (100 + markup) × 100.
Is 50% markup the same as 50% margin?
No. 50% markup on $40 gives a $60 price and a 33.33% margin. A 50% margin on a $60 price would need a $30 cost. Confusing the two is the most expensive pricing mistake a small business makes.
What if I want a target margin instead?
Work backwards: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin ÷ 100). For a 40% margin on a $40 cost, price = $40 ÷ 0.60 = $66.67.
Should tax be in the cost or added later?
Added later, on the selling price. Mixing sales tax into cost distorts both markup and margin; keep the price tax-exclusive here and apply tax at checkout.
Yes — luxury and low-cost goods often do. A 200% markup triples the cost: $40 becomes $120, with a 66.67% margin.
No. A discount comes off the selling price after markup. Price first with markup, then apply the markdown to see the final profit.

Central tendency of a data set: mean, median, and mode, with the sorted data, sum, count, and range shown alongside.
The three central-tendency measures of a data set — mean, median, and mode — with the sorted data, sum, count, and range alongside.
Numbers, separated by commas or spaces
Results update as you type. Non-numeric entries are ignored. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Mean = sum of all values ÷ count. Median = the middle value of the sorted data (or the average of the two middle values when the count is even). Mode = the value that appears most often; a data set can have several modes, or none when every value appears once.

Data 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 8, 9: sorted, that is 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9. Sum = 43, count = 7, so mean = 43 ÷ 7 = 6.14. The middle (4th) value is 6, so the median is 6. The value 8 appears twice — more than any other — so the mode is 8. Range = 9 − 3 = 6.

These are descriptive measures of the data you enter — they describe this set, not a wider population, and they say nothing about spread on their own (pair them with range or standard deviation for that). The mean is pulled by outliers: one very large value raises it even when most values are small, which is exactly when the median is the better summary. Modes are only meaningful for data where repeats are expected; with continuous measurements, exact repeats are rare and the mode may not exist.
Mean or median — which should I report?

Report the mean for roughly symmetric data and the median when the data is skewed or has outliers. Income is the classic case: a few very high incomes raise the mean well above what a typical person earns, so median income is the standard headline figure.
What if there are two middle values?
With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values. For 2, 4, 7, 9 the median is (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.50.
Can there be more than one mode?
Yes. If two values tie for the highest frequency, the data is bimodal and both are modes. This page lists all tied values.
Every value appears exactly once, so nothing is most frequent. That is common with continuous measurements like heights recorded to the millimetre.
Do I need to sort the data first?
No. Sorting is done for you; the median and the sorted list are computed from whatever order you paste in.
No. Commas, spaces, and line breaks all work as separators, so pasted spreadsheet columns work directly.

What a recurring meeting really costs in staff time value: per meeting, per week, and over the year.
Person-hours = people × minutes ÷ 60, scaled by meetings per week and working weeks.

Annual time value = people × hourly cost × meeting minutes ÷ 60 × weekly meetings × working weeks. Cost per meeting = people × hourly cost × minutes ÷ 60. Cost per week = cost per meeting × weekly meetings.

9 people at $180/hour for 60 minutes: cost per meeting = 9 × 180 × 60 ÷ 60 = $1,620. At 3 meetings per week that is $4,860 per week, and over 48 working weeks the annual time value is $1,620 × 3 × 48 = $233,280, or 1,296 person-hours per year. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

This is an opportunity-cost estimate based on the average hourly cost you enter, not necessarily an avoidable cash expense: salaried staff are paid whether or not they attend. Preparation time is included only if you add it to the meeting length. Room, tooling, and travel costs are not included. The hourly figure should be a fully loaded cost (salary plus on-costs) if the result is meant to represent total staff cost.
Is this a cash saving if I cancel the meeting?
Not necessarily. It is the value of staff time freed up. Cash is saved only if that time would otherwise be paid overtime or contractor time.
Should the hourly rate include on-costs?
Yes, if you want total staff cost. Use a fully loaded rate — salary plus benefits, payroll taxes and overhead — rather than base pay alone.
Add it to the meeting length, or run a second calculation for preparation and add the two results.
It is the example assumption (52 weeks less holidays and leave). Change it to match your own calendar.
Does a shorter meeting save proportionally?
In this model, yes: cost scales linearly with minutes, people, and frequency, so halving any one of them halves the cost.

Mass of one mole of a compound from its chemical formula — with the elemental composition alongside.
Element symbols with counts; parentheses allowed, e.g. Ca(OH)2. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Molar mass = Σ (count of each element × that element's atomic weight). Atomic weights are the standard relative atomic masses: H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007, O 15.999, and so on. Parentheses multiply everything inside them, so Ca(OH)2 means one calcium plus two of everything in (OH): Ca + 2 × O + 2 × H. The result is in grams per mole (g/mol).

Water, H2O: 2 × 1.008 (hydrogen) + 1 × 15.999 (oxygen) = 2.016 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. So one mole of water — 6.022 × 10²³ molecules — weighs 18.015 grams, about a tablespoon. By composition, water is 2.016 ÷ 18.015 = 11.19% hydrogen and 15.999 ÷ 18.015 = 88.81% oxygen by mass. Other checks: CO2 = 12.011 + 2 × 15.999 = 44.009 g/mol; table salt NaCl = 22.990 + 35.45 = 58.440 g/mol.

This page covers common elements with standard atomic weights; it does not handle charges (ions), isotopes (deuterated water needs D as a separate entry, which is not included), hydrates written with a dot (write CuSO4·5H2O as CuSO4H10O5 instead), or structural formulas. Atomic weights are averages over natural isotope abundances, so they vary slightly by source — the third decimal may differ between tables. For laboratory work, confirm against your reference table; for teaching and estimation, these values are standard.
A counting unit: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). Molar mass connects that count to something weighable — the grams in one mole of a substance.

Because atomic weights are not whole numbers: hydrogen averages 1.008 (mostly H-1 with a little heavier H-2) and oxygen 15.999. Whole-number masses are a school shortcut; 18.015 is the standard value.
The number after a closing parenthesis multiplies everything inside it. In Ca(OH)2, the 2 doubles both O and H: Ca + O2 + H2, giving 40.078 + 2 × 15.999 + 2 × 1.008 = 74.092 g/mol.
What if my element is not recognised?

The page lists the elements it knows and reports unknown symbols instead of guessing. The table covers the elements most formulas use; rare earths and synthetics are left out deliberately rather than given approximate weights.
How do I use molar mass in practice?
To convert mass to moles, divide grams by molar mass; to convert moles to mass, multiply. For example, 36.03 g of water is 36.03 ÷ 18.015 = 2.00 moles.
Is molar mass the same as molecular weight?
Numerically yes, units differ: molecular weight is a relative number (unitless), molar mass is that number expressed in g/mol. People use the terms interchangeably in most contexts.

Bars are scaled to the total monthly payment. Principal & interest is usually the largest slice; tax and insurance are estimates from the annual figures you enter.

Loan = home price − down payment. Loan-to-value = loan ÷ home price. Principal & interest uses the standard amortization formula on the loan amount. PMI applies only when loan-to-value exceeds 80%, at loan × PMI rate ÷ 12 per month. Tax and insurance are annual figures ÷ 12.

Home price $400,000 with $80,000 down: loan $320,000, loan-to-value 80.00%. At 6.5% for 30 years, principal & interest is $2,022.62. Add tax $400.00 and insurance $125.00 a month; PMI is $0 because loan-to-value does not exceed 80%. Total monthly payment $2,547.62.

Fixed rate for the whole term, PMI charged at a flat rate while loan-to-value exceeds 80% (real PMI usually drops off and is repriced), and no closing costs, points, or rate adjustments. Tax and insurance are assumed constant; in practice both change over time. Extra principal shortens the loan but is not included in the headline total above.
Here, only when the loan exceeds 80% of the home price. At exactly 80% there is no PMI in this model. Lenders also apply their own PMI rules and cancellation thresholds.
Is the extra principal part of the total?
No. The headline total is the required monthly bill. Extra principal is voluntary and is shown separately so the required payment stays comparable.
Why is the loan amount not the home price?
The down payment is paid upfront, so only the remainder is borrowed. A larger down payment lowers both the loan and the monthly payment.
Do tax and insurance stay fixed?
No. Both typically change year to year; this calculator spreads the annual figures you enter evenly across months.
No. Closing costs are paid at purchase and are not part of the monthly payment. The refinance calculator models them separately.

Estimate take-home pay from gross pay, an effective tax rate you enter, and your deductions — no jurisdiction's tax rates are assumed.
All figures are monthly unless labeled per year. The tax rate is an effective rate you enter — it is not any jurisdiction's statutory rate.
Net pay plus deductions equals gross pay. A longer deductions bar means less than half of gross pay reaches you.
Net pay at different effective tax rates
Gross pay and other deductions are held at the values above; only the tax rate changes across rows.
Estimated tax = gross pay × effective tax rate. Net pay = gross pay − estimated tax − social contributions − other deductions. Net pay per year = net pay per month × 12.

Gross pay $6,000 per month, effective tax rate 15%, social contributions $500, other deductions $0: estimated tax = $6,000 × 0.15 = $900, net pay = $6,000 − $900 − $500 − $0 = $4,600 per month, or $55,200 per year.

Tax systems vary by location and personal circumstances: brackets, allowances, credits, employer contributions, and benefits are not modeled. Enter an effective rate from your own payslip or payroll calculation and verify important figures against an official payroll calculation. This is an estimate, not a payroll or tax filing.
How does the net salary calculator work?
Net pay = gross pay − estimated tax − social contributions − other deductions, where estimated tax = gross pay × the effective tax rate you enter.
What effective tax rate should I enter?

Your actual tax divided by your gross pay from a recent payslip, or a rate your payroll department confirms. No country or region's rate is pre-filled, because statutory rates and brackets differ too much to assume.
Why is net pay negative in my calculation?
Deductions exceed gross pay at the values entered. Check the rate and deduction amounts — a negative result flags an input problem, not a real payslip.
No. Only deductions from your gross pay are counted. Employer-side contributions are a separate cost and do not reduce your net pay here.
Does this handle bonuses or overtime?
Only if you fold them into the monthly gross pay you enter. Irregular pay should be averaged or calculated for the specific month.
Can I use this for tax filing?
No. It is a take-home estimate. Filing depends on your jurisdiction's full rules, allowances, and credits.

Solve any variable of Ohm's law — voltage, current, resistance, or power — from the other two, with power shown alongside.
Solve for voltage, current, resistance, or power from the other two — V = IR and P = VI, for DC circuits and resistive AC loads.
The two input labels change with the chosen unknown. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

V = I × R, and P = V × I. From those two, every other form follows: I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I, P = I² × R, P = V² ÷ R. The "Check" chip recomputes the solved value through the other relation to confirm consistency.
Solve for current with V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.00 A. Power = V × I = 12 × 3 = 36.00 W. Check through the other form: P = V² ÷ R = 144 ÷ 4 = 36.00 W — consistent.

This is DC and resistive AC: it assumes voltage and current are in phase and resistance is constant. It does not cover reactive AC circuits (inductors, capacitors, phase shift) or temperature-dependent resistance — a filament lamp's resistance rises sharply as it heats, so cold resistance gives a misleading current. Zero resistance means a short circuit: current is unbounded in the ideal model, so the page refuses division by zero rather than showing infinity. Real circuits always have some resistance and a supply with a current limit.
Which two values do I need?
Any two of voltage, current, and resistance determine the third — and power follows from any voltage-current pair. Pick the unknown above and enter the two you know.
Why does the page refuse zero resistance?
Because I = V ÷ R with R = 0 is a short circuit: the ideal model predicts infinite current. Real supplies limit current or fail; no finite answer exists, so the page says so.
Does this work for AC mains?
For resistive loads (heaters, incandescent lamps) yes, using RMS voltage and current. For motors and electronics with inductance or capacitance, use impedance and phase-aware calculations instead.
What is the power rating warning about?
A resistor converts power to heat. A 36 W result through a 0.25 W resistor would destroy it — always check the component's power rating against the computed power, not just the resistance value.
Volts, amps, ohms — which unit scale?
Base SI units here: volts, amps, ohms, watts. For milliamps, divide by 1,000 first (500 mA = 0.5 A); for kilohms, multiply by 1,000 (4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω).
Can I solve for power directly?
Yes: choose Power and enter voltage and current. The page also shows the implied resistance (V ÷ I) as the check value.

Pace per kilometre, pace per mile, and average speed from distance and finish time — an average that ignores pauses, terrain, and elevation.
Pace bars are labels, not comparisons: a mile is longer than a kilometre, so the per-mile time is always larger at the same speed.
Total time = hours × 3,600 + minutes × 60 + seconds. Pace per kilometre = total time ÷ distance (km). Pace per mile = pace per kilometre × 1.609344. Speed = distance ÷ total hours.
Distance 10 km, finish time 50 minutes (3,000 seconds): pace = 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300 seconds =
(7.46 mph). At the same pace, 5 km takes 25:00 and a marathon takes 3:30:59. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

The result is a single average over the whole distance: it assumes perfectly even pacing and ignores pauses, terrain, weather, elevation, and GPS measurement error, all of which make real splits vary. Projected times for other distances assume the same pace can be held, which becomes less realistic as distance grows.
Why is the per-mile pace slower than per-kilometre?
Because a mile (1.609344 km) is longer than a kilometre, so it takes proportionally longer at the same speed.
Does this account for hills or stops?
No. It divides total elapsed time by distance, so pauses and terrain are averaged into the single pace figure.
How accurate is a projected marathon time?
Only as an arithmetic projection: holding a 10 km pace for 42.195 km is much harder than holding it for 10 km, so treat projections as reference numbers.
What if my time includes seconds over 59?
Enter them as minutes instead — the seconds field is capped at 59, matching how times are normally written.
Can I use miles as the distance input?
Convert first: divide miles by 0.621371 to get kilometres, or multiply kilometres by 0.621371 to go the other way.

Bars are scaled to the larger of the two amounts. Waste is the extra paint on top of the exact coats calculation.
Paint required by number of coats
Same area, coverage and waste allowance; only the coat count changes.
Paint per coat = area ÷ coverage per litre. Paint for all coats = area × coats ÷ coverage per litre. Paint required = paint for all coats × (1 + waste rate).

Area 120 m², 2 coats, coverage 10 m²/L: paint per coat = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 L, so 2 coats need 24 L. At a 10% waste allowance, waste = 24 × 0.10 = 2.4 L, giving 26.4 L required. These are the example defaults above; replace them with your own area and the coverage printed on your paint.

Coverage varies with surface porosity, primer, application method (brush, roller, spray), colour change and the manufacturer's stated rate — the coverage you enter should come from your paint's own data sheet. Doors, windows and trim must be subtracted from the area yourself if you do not intend to paint them. No can size or price is assumed: divide the result by your can size to get the number of cans.
How does the paint calculator work?
Paint required = area × coats ÷ coverage per litre × (1 + waste rate). Every input is yours; nothing here is a market average.
Should I include primer in the coats?
Only if the primer is the same product at the same coverage. Otherwise calculate primer separately with its own coverage rate.
Why does coverage vary so much?
Porous or unprimed surfaces absorb more paint, dark-to-light colour changes need more coats, and spray application loses more to overspray than a roller does.
How many cans do I need?
Divide the required litres by the size of the can you buy and round up. Can sizes differ by product and region, so no can size is built into this page.
Do I subtract doors and windows?
Yes, if you are not painting them. Measure the wall area, then subtract the area of openings you will leave unpainted.
