A fast, transparent percentage calculator with instant results: a percentage of a value, and that value after an increase or decrease.
Enter a percentage and a base value.
Percentage of base = base value × percentage ÷ 100. Value after increase = base × (1 + percentage ÷ 100). Value after decrease = base × (1 − percentage ÷ 100).
15% of 280 = 280 × 15 ÷ 100 = 42. After a 15% increase: 280 + 42 = 322. After a 15% decrease: 280 − 42 = 238. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result, then replace the values with your own.

Percentages may be negative or above 100; a decrease larger than 100% gives a negative result, which is arithmetically correct but may not be meaningful for the quantity being described. Results are rounded to 2 decimal places for display. This page computes percentages only — it does not add tax, fees, or compounding unless those are part of the percentage you enter.
How is a percentage of a value calculated?
Multiply the base by the percentage and divide by 100. For example, 15% of 280 is 280 × 15 ÷ 100 = 42.
The base plus the percentage amount: 280 increased by 15% is 280 + 42 = 322.

This page takes the hydrogen ion concentration as given; it does not work out how much a weak acid dissociates, which needs the acid's equilibrium constant. The pH + pOH = 14 relation holds at 25 °C; at other temperatures the neutral point shifts (at 100 °C, neutral pH is about 6.14). Activity effects in concentrated solutions are ignored, so results are exact for dilute solutions and approximate for strong ones. This page is for calculation, not for handling chemicals — follow lab safety rules for real solutions.
Because concentrations span many orders of magnitude: stomach acid at pH 2 has 10,000 times the hydrogen ions of a pH 6 solution, not three times. Each whole pH step means a tenfold change.
Only at 25 °C. Neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], and that balance point moves with temperature, so neutral water at 100 °C has pH 6.14.
Can pH be negative or above 14?
Yes, for very concentrated acids or bases — a 10 mol/L strong acid has a nominal pH of −1. The 0–14 range is a rule of thumb for dilute solutions, not a law.
What is the difference between pH and pOH?
Two views of the same solution: pH tracks hydrogen ions, pOH tracks hydroxide ions. At 25 °C they always add to 14, so either one determines the other.
Why does my measured pH differ from the calculated one?

Meters measure activity, not concentration; temperature, calibration, and dissolved salts all shift readings. For weak acids, incomplete dissociation is usually the bigger cause — the concentration you put in is not the free [H⁺].
What is a familiar reference point?
Pure water pH 7, coffee about 5, vinegar about 2.4, baking soda solution about 8.3, household bleach about 12.5.

Naegele’s rule is an estimate built on two assumptions that often do not hold exactly: a regular 28-day cycle and ovulation on day 14. Adding 280 days (40 weeks) to the first day of the last menstrual period. It is the standard back-of-the-envelope dating rule, not a measurement.
Why might the real date differ?
Because cycles vary: ovulation is not always on day 14, cycle lengths differ, and the LMP date itself can be uncertain. Ultrasound dating often refines the estimate.
What if my cycles are longer than 28 days?
Then ovulation likely came later than day 14, and the true due date may be later than this estimate. The page does not adjust for cycle length — that adjustment belongs in clinical dating.
Does the due date mean the baby will arrive that day?
No. It is an estimate at the centre of a range; actual delivery dates vary widely around it.
Should I use this for medical decisions?

Today's value of a future sum at a given discount rate — the time value of money, with the discount amount shown alongside.
What a future sum is worth today at a given discount rate — the time value of money, with the discount amount shown alongside.
Annual compounding. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

, where FV is the future sum, r is the annual discount rate as a decimal, and n is the number of years. The discount is FV − PV: the amount the future sum loses by waiting. This is the mirror image of compound growth — the future value formula run backwards.
$10,000 due in 10 years at a 5% discount rate: PV = 10,000 ÷ 1.05
= 10,000 ÷ 1.6289 = $6,139.13. The discount is 10,000 − 6,139.13 = $3,860.87. At 5 years instead, the same sum is worth 10,000 ÷ 1.05
= $7,835.26 — waiting twice as long costs more than twice the discount, because compounding accelerates.

This page discounts a single lump sum at a constant annual rate with annual compounding. It does not handle a series of payments (that needs an annuity calculation), a changing rate over time, monthly compounding, taxes, or inflation adjustments — a nominal discount rate and a real (inflation-adjusted) rate give different answers. The rate you pick is doing all the work: a small change in r moves the present value a lot over long horizons, so treat the result as a comparison tool, not a market price.
Why is a future sum worth less today?

Because money today can be invested and grown. $6,139.13 invested at 5% for 10 years becomes $10,000, so the two amounts are equivalent at that rate — neither is a bargain, they are the same value at different times.

It depends on the question. For an investment decision, use your expected return or cost of capital. For comparing offers, use the same rate for every option so the comparison is fair. There is no single correct rate.
How is this different from the future value calculator?
They are inverses. Future value grows a present sum forward (multiply by (1 + r)
); present value discounts a future sum back (divide by (1 + r)
Does a higher rate raise or lower present value?
Lower. A higher discount rate means future money is penalised more heavily, so its present value falls. At 10% instead of 5%, the same $10,000 in 10 years is worth only $3,855.43.
With monthly compounding the divisor becomes (1 + r/12)
, which makes the present value slightly smaller than the annual-compounding figure. This page uses annual compounding and says so; for monthly schedules, adjust the rate and periods accordingly.

Only if the future amount is negative (a future payment you must make). A future receipt always discounts to a positive present value. If you are valuing a future liability, enter it as a positive amount and read the result as the amount to set aside today.

Model how a price increase changes profit when some volume is lost.
Model how a price increase changes profit when volume falls — enter the price, cost, sales, increase, and expected volume decline.
The volume decline is the decline you expect, entered directly — it is not predicted from an elasticity coefficient. See the FAQ for how the source scenario labels this input.
Bars are scaled to the larger profit. A shorter new-profit bar means the increase loses money despite the higher price.
Profit change at different volume declines
Price, cost, sales, and the price increase are held at the values above; only the volume decline changes across rows.

New price = price × (1 + increase%). New volume = sales × (1 − volume decline%). New profit = (new price − cost) × new volume. Current profit = (price − cost) × sales. Profit change = new profit − current profit.

Price $199, cost $110, sales 1,000 units, increase 8%, volume decline 5%: new price = $199 × 1.08 = $214.92, new volume = 1,000 × 0.95 = 950 units, new profit = ($214.92 − $110) × 950 = $99,674, current profit = ($199 − $110) × 1,000 = $89,000, so profit rises by $10,674.

Unit cost stays constant and the volume decline is entered by you, not predicted. Fixed costs, competitor responses, customer switching over time, and demand shifts are not modeled — treat the result as a scenario comparison, not a forecast.
Profit change = (price × (1 + increase%) − cost) × sales × (1 − volume decline%) − (price − cost) × sales. The new margin per unit times the new volume, minus today's profit.
What does the volume decline input mean?

The percentage of sales volume you expect to lose after the increase, entered directly. The source scenario labels this field elasticity, but the formula uses the entered percentage itself as the decline — it does not multiply an elasticity coefficient by the price increase.
Can a price increase lose money?
Yes. If the volume lost outweighs the extra margin per unit, new profit falls below current profit. That is exactly the trade this calculator exposes.
Why is unit cost held constant?
Volume changes can move unit cost in reality, but this model isolates the price-volume trade. If your unit cost changes with volume, adjust the cost input and compare scenarios.
They cancel out of the change: both scenarios bear the same fixed costs, so the difference in profit is driven by unit margin and volume alone.
Should I use this as a pricing decision on its own?
No. Combine it with customer research, competitor pricing, and a margin check — the volume decline you enter is the most uncertain input, so test several values.

Bars are scaled to the larger of total cost and profit. When costs exceed revenue, the profit bar is shown in amber and the verdict flags the loss.
Costs are held at the values above; only revenue changes across rows.
Net profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs. Net margin = net profit ÷ revenue × 100%. Total cost = variable costs + fixed costs. Cost ratio = total cost ÷ revenue × 100%.

Revenue $100,000, variable costs $68,000, fixed costs $8,000: total cost = $76,000, net profit = $100,000 − $76,000 = $24,000, net margin = $24,000 ÷ $100,000 × 100% = 24.00%, and cost ratio = 76.00%.

This is an operating view: interest, taxes, depreciation, and one-off items are not separated out. If your cost figures already include them, the margin reflects that; if not, it does not. Costs are treated as fixed totals for the period, not per-unit rates.
How does the profit calculator work?
Net profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs; net margin = net profit ÷ revenue. It splits a period's revenue into what costs consumed and what remained.
What is the difference between variable and fixed costs?
Variable costs move with output — materials, per-order fees. Fixed costs do not — rent, base salaries. The split matters for break-even analysis; for net profit only the total matters.
What does a negative net profit mean?
Costs exceeded revenue for the period: a loss of that amount. The margin is negative by the same proportion.
Is net margin the same as gross margin?
No. Gross margin stops at cost of goods sold; net margin counts all variable and fixed costs entered here, so it is usually lower.
No, unless tax is already inside the cost figures you enter. Apply tax treatment separately to the net profit.
Why does margin show a dash at zero revenue?
Margin divides by revenue, so at zero revenue it is undefined. Profit itself is still shown as negative total costs.
Solve ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero: both roots, the discriminant, the vertex, and complex roots when the discriminant is negative.
Roots of ax² + bx + c = 0, with the discriminant, the vertex, and complex roots when the discriminant is negative.
x² − 5x + 6 = 0: a = 1, b = −5, c = 6. Discriminant = (−5)² − 4 × 1 × 6 = 25 − 24 = 1. Roots = [5 ± √1] ÷ 2, so x = 3 and x = 2. Check: 3² − 15 + 6 = 0 and 2² − 10 + 6 = 0. The vertex is at x = 2.5.

Only genuine quadratics are solved: a must not be zero. If a = 0 the equation is linear (bx + c = 0) and this page says so instead of dividing by zero. Coefficients may be decimals or negative. Very large coefficients can lose precision in floating-point arithmetic; results are rounded to two decimals for display, so a root like 0.001 may show as 0.
Then it is not a quadratic at all — it is the linear equation bx + c = 0, with the single solution x = −c ÷ b (when b is not zero either). This page flags that case instead of producing nonsense.
What does the discriminant tell me?
Whether the roots are real and how many: positive means two distinct real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means no real roots — the parabola never crosses the x-axis.

When the discriminant is negative, the roots involve i (the square root of −1). For x² + 2x + 5 = 0 the roots are −1 + 2i and −1 − 2i. They are genuine solutions over the complex numbers, just not points on the real x-axis.
A degree-2 polynomial has two roots counting multiplicity. They can coincide (one repeated root) or be a complex pair, but there are always two.
Factoring is faster when the roots are small integers, as in the example (x − 3)(x − 2). The formula always works, including when factoring is not obvious.

Is a lower payment always a win?

What if I move before break-even?

Then the savings never repay the closing costs. Enter your planned stay above and the verdict checks this for you: a refinance that breaks even after your move is flagged, even if the monthly saving looks good.
Does refinancing reset my payoff date?

Cash saving is commute spending saved minus extra home costs. Time value is recovered hours times hourly value. The total combines both.
Bars compare the cash half with the time half. The cash bar is floored at zero for display when cash saving is negative — the table shows the true figure.
Each row reuses your daily commute figures and hourly value and varies only remote days. Home costs are monthly and fixed, so few remote days look worse per day.
Monthly value = remote days × (daily commute spending + commute minutes ÷ 60 × hourly value) − extra home costs. Cash saving = remote days × daily commute spending − extra home costs.

Commute $45 per day, 90 minutes per day, hourly value $80, 12 remote days, extra home costs $300. Per day: $45 + 90 ÷ 60 × $80 = $45 + $120 = $165. Gross = 12 × $165 = $1,980. Total = $1,980 − $300 = $1,680 per month. Cash-only (hourly value zero): 12 × $45 − $300 = $240 per month. Recovered time = 12 × 1.5 = 18 hours.

Set hourly value to zero for a cash-only comparison: recovered time is not automatically spendable income, and valuing it at full hourly cost overstates the benefit if it is absorbed by household tasks or rest. Extra home costs are a single monthly figure — heating, electricity, equipment, and food increases must all be inside it or the cash saving is overstated. Each remote day is worth daily commute spending plus commute minutes divided by 60 times hourly value; multiply by remote days and subtract extra monthly home costs.
Is the time value real money?
Only if the recovered time earns or saves money. For a cash-only view, set hourly value to zero — the worked example's cash-only figure is $240, not $1,680.
What counts as extra home costs?
The increase in heating, electricity, internet, equipment, and food caused by working from home, for the month. If you would pay most of it anyway, do not count it.
Why do few remote days look bad?
Because home costs are monthly and fixed while savings scale with days. One remote day a month rarely covers a full month of extra home costs on cash alone.
Should I count the commute both ways?
Yes: minutes and spending should be the full round trip for the day, not one leg. Halving either input halves the daily value.
Does this include wellbeing or career effects?
No. Less commuting may improve wellbeing and focus, while less office presence may affect visibility and collaboration. Those are real but outside this money-and-time model.

Orders 3,000, return rate 12%, profit per order $45, reverse shipping $18, returned value $120, loss 25%: returned orders = 3,000 × 0.12 = 360, erosion per return = $45 + $18 + $120 × 0.25 = $93, and total erosion = 360 × $93 = $33,480.

Profit erosion = orders × return rate% × (profit per order + reverse shipping + returned value × loss%). Each return costs the profit it would have kept, plus shipping it back, plus the share of product value written off.
What does the loss percentage mean?
The share of a returned product's value that cannot be recovered — damage, missing parts, or unsellable condition. A 25% loss on a $120 item is $30 per return.
Eroded profit divided by the profit all orders would have earned with no returns. At the example values it is $33,480 ÷ $135,000 = 24.80%.
Only if your profit-per-order figure already deducts reverse shipping. If it does, set reverse shipping to $0 or adjust the profit figure — the FAQ and scope note flag this.
What about returns that are resold?
Not modeled: a resold return recovers most of the product value, so the loss percentage for those units should be near zero. Use a blended loss rate across all returns.

Missing sides and angles of a right triangle from its two legs — hypotenuse, angles, area, and perimeter.
The two sides meeting at the right angle. All lengths in the same unit. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Pythagoras: hypotenuse c = √(a² + b²). The acute angles come from the sides: the angle opposite leg a is arctan(a ÷ b), and the angle opposite leg b is 90° minus that angle — the two acute angles always add to 90°. Area = ½ × a × b, and perimeter = a + b + c.

Legs 3 and 4: hypotenuse = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. The angle opposite the side of 3 is arctan(3 ÷ 4) = 36.87°, so the other acute angle is 90 − 36.87 = 53.13°. Area = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6, and perimeter = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. The 3–4–5 triangle is the smallest right triangle with whole-number sides, which is why it shows up everywhere from building sites to textbook problems.

This page takes the two legs of a right triangle. It does not solve triangles given a hypotenuse and one leg, or given an angle and a side — for those, use Pythagoras or trigonometry directly on the same formulas above. It assumes the angle between the two entered sides is exactly 90°; for any other triangle, these formulas do not apply. Angles display in degrees to two decimals.

It is Pythagoras' theorem: in a right triangle, the square built on the hypotenuse has the same area as the two squares built on the legs combined. It holds for every right triangle, not just whole-number ones.

The smallest right triangle with whole-number sides: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². Builders have used knotted ropes in 3–4–5 proportions for millennia to lay out exact right angles, since any multiple (6–8–10, 9–12–15) works the same way.

From the ratio of the legs: the angle opposite leg a satisfies tan(angle) = a ÷ b, so angle = arctan(a ÷ b). The second acute angle is 90° minus the first, because a triangle's angles sum to 180° and the right angle already takes 90°.
Can I enter the hypotenuse instead of a leg?
Not on this page — it expects the two legs. If you know the hypotenuse c and one leg a, the other leg is √(c² − a²), which you can compute and then enter here.
Only that both legs use the same unit: the hypotenuse, area, and perimeter then come out in that unit and its square. Mixing metres and centimetres gives a wrong answer, so convert first.
Pythagoras does not apply. General triangles need the law of cosines (c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C) or the triangle area calculator's Heron formula, depending on what you know.

Measure investment gain or loss relative to the initial amount invested — ending value plus cash income, compared with what you put in.
Gain is what you end up with, minus what you put in. Cash income counts only if you actually received it.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two amounts. A gain bar longer than the initial bar means a positive ROI.

ROI = (ending value + cash income − initial investment) ÷ initial investment × 100%. Gain = ending value + cash income − initial investment.

ROI does not account for how long capital was invested, so it cannot fairly compare investments held for different periods — use an annualized return for that. Taxes, fees, and inflation are not included unless they are already reflected in the values you enter.
How does the ROI calculator work?
ROI = (ending value + cash income − initial investment) ÷ initial investment × 100%. It answers one question: for each dollar invested, how much came back above the original stake?
A negative ROI means ending value plus cash income is less than the initial investment — you got back less than you put in. The size of the loss is the gain figure shown as a negative amount.
Can I compare two investments with ROI alone?
Only if they were held for the same length of time. A 30% return over one year beats 30% over five years. For different holding periods, compare annualized returns instead.
Yes, if you received it — dividends, interest, or rent paid out during the holding period are part of the return. Do not double-count income that is already reflected in the final value.
Does ROI include taxes or fees?
No, unless the values you enter already reflect them. Brokerage fees, taxes on gains, and inflation all reduce the real return.
Is a high ROI always better?
Not necessarily. ROI says nothing about risk, volatility, or how long the money was tied up. A high ROI on a risky, illiquid investment is not directly comparable to a lower ROI on a safe one.

Balance by year on this plan

Target $50,000 in 5 years, starting from $5,000 at 3%: the $5,000 grows to $5,808.08, leaving a gap of $44,191.92. Spread over 60 end-of-month contributions at 0.25% a month, the required contribution is $44,191.92 ÷ 64.65 = $683.59 a month.

Why does a higher rate lower the monthly amount?

End of the month, matching the source calculator. Starting a month earlier would lower the required amount slightly.
Should the target be adjusted for inflation?

What if I cannot afford the required amount?

Estimate how many months it takes a side hustle to recover its startup cost from monthly contribution.
Estimate how many months a side hustle takes to recover its startup cost from monthly contribution after fixed costs.
Monthly contribution is profit per order times monthly orders minus monthly fixed costs. Break-even divides the startup cost by that contribution.
Bars compare the startup cost with a full year of contribution. If the year bar clears the startup bar, break-even falls inside 12 months.
Each row is cumulative contribution minus the startup cost, assuming the same orders, profit, and fixed costs throughout. Early months are negative until the startup cost is recovered.

Months to break even = startup cost ÷ (profit per order × monthly orders − monthly fixed costs). Orders to recover the cost = startup cost ÷ profit per order. Net after N months = monthly contribution × N − startup cost.

Startup $20,000, fixed costs $1,200 per month, profit $85 per order, 60 orders per month. Monthly contribution = $85 × 60 − $1,200 = $5,100 − $1,200 = $3,900. Months to break even = $20,000 ÷ $3,900 = 5.13 months. Orders to recover the cost = $20,000 ÷ $85 = 235.29 orders. Net after 12 months = $3,900 × 12 − $20,000 = $26,800.

Monthly contribution must be positive for any break-even to exist; if fixed costs exceed gross contribution, the model reports no break-even rather than a negative time. Sales and margins are assumptions, not guaranteed demand, and the model assumes they stay constant — seasonality, churn, price changes, and growth are not modeled. Financing costs, tax, payment timing, refunds, and the value of the founder's time are excluded unless folded into fixed costs or profit per order.
Monthly contribution is profit per order times monthly orders minus monthly fixed costs; months to break even are the startup cost divided by that contribution.
What if contribution is zero or negative?

Then there is no break-even: the hustle loses money or stands still every month, and the startup cost is never recovered. Fix contribution first — more orders, higher profit per order, or lower fixed costs.
Does break-even mean profitable from then on?
It means the startup cost has been repaid. From that month onward, monthly contribution is profit before tax and before the founder's time, if neither is counted in the inputs.
Should founder time be in fixed costs?
If you want an honest answer, yes — value the hours at a reasonable rate and include them, or the break-even flatters a hustle that only works by donating unpaid labour.
Why does the order count have a fraction?
235.29 orders is the arithmetic answer; in practice it means the 236th order is the one that tips the cumulative total past the startup cost, part-way through the break-even month.
Financing, tax, refunds, seasonality, and demand risk. Treat the month count as a planning figure at assumed sales, and re-run it at half sales to see the downside case.

How is simple interest different from compound interest?
Simple interest is always calculated on the original principal. Compound interest is calculated on principal plus previously earned interest, so it grows faster over time.
When is simple interest actually used?
For some short-term loans, car loans with simple-interest terms, and textbook interest problems. Most savings accounts and mortgages compound instead.
Does the interest stay the same every year?
Yes, as long as the principal and rate do not change. That is the defining feature of simple interest.

Enter at least one number, separated by commas or spaces.

Population or sample SD — which do I use?
Population SD (÷ n) when your numbers are the whole group you care about. Sample SD (÷ n − 1) when they are a sample and you are estimating the spread of a larger population.

Solve two linear equations for x and y by the determinant method, with a check of both equations.
Find the x and y that satisfy two linear equations at once — by the determinant method, with both equations checked.
Equation 1: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ · Equation 2: a₂x + b₂y = c₂

For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂, let D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁. If D ≠ 0, there is exactly one solution: x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁) ÷ D and y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁) ÷ D. This is Cramer's rule for two equations. If D = 0, the lines are parallel or identical: parallel lines never meet (no solution), identical lines meet everywhere (infinitely many solutions).

2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2: D = 2 × (−1) − 1 × 1 = −3. Then x = (7 × (−1) − 2 × 1) ÷ (−3) = (−9) ÷ (−3) = 3, and y = (2 × 2 − 1 × 7) ÷ (−3) = (−3) ÷ (−3) = 1. Check: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, and 3 − 1 = 2. Both equations hold, so (3, 1) is the single crossing point of the two lines.

This page solves two linear equations in two unknowns. It does not handle three or more equations, nonlinear terms (x², xy), or inequalities. When D = 0 it distinguishes the two cases: if the equations are proportional (same line), it reports infinitely many solutions; otherwise it reports no solution. Results display to two decimals; repeating decimals such as 1/3 show as 0.33, so keep the fraction form for exact work.
What does the solution mean geometrically?

Each equation is a straight line, and the solution is their crossing point. One crossing means one solution; parallel lines never cross (no solution); the same line twice means every point on it works (infinitely many solutions).
What if the determinant is zero?

Then the two lines have the same slope. The page checks proportionality: if one equation is a multiple of the other, the lines coincide and every point on the line is a solution; otherwise they are distinct parallels with no solution at all.
Why is it called Cramer's rule?
After Gabriel Cramer, who published the determinant method in 1750. It is the same elimination you would do by hand — multiply, subtract, solve — compressed into two formulas.
Can I solve by substitution instead?

Yes, and you should get the same answer. From x − y = 2, x = y + 2; substituting into 2x + y = 7 gives 2(y + 2) + y = 7, so 3y = 3, y = 1, x = 3. Substitution is easier by hand for simple systems; determinants scale better.
Do the two equations have to be linear?
Yes for this method. If either equation contains x², y², xy, or a square root of x or y, the determinant formulas do not apply, and the system can have zero, one, two, or more solutions.
How do I check my answer?
Substitute x and y back into both original equations, as the page's check chips do. A correct solution makes both sides equal in both equations; a solution that satisfies only one equation is wrong.

TDEE inherits the limits of both parts: BMR is a population equation that varies between individuals, and the activity factor is a coarse category chosen by judgment, not a measurement of actual days. Two people picking the same label can have quite different true activity, and day-to-day variation is averaged away. The result is a planning estimate, not a measured daily burn.
What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
BMR is resting expenditure only. TDEE multiplies BMR by an activity factor to include everything else a day involves.
How do I pick an activity level?

Judge a typical week honestly: mostly sitting is sedentary, light daily movement is lightly active, regular training is moderately active, hard daily training is very active. When in doubt, the lower category is the more cautious estimate.
Why does the category change the result so much?
Because the factor multiplies the whole BMR: moving from 1.2 to 1.9 raises the example result by about 58%, so a wrong category is the largest error source on this page.

Area of a triangle from base and height, or from three sides with Heron's formula — with perimeter alongside.
Area from base and height — or from three sides with Heron's formula — with the perimeter alongside.
All lengths in the same unit. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

From base and height: area = ½ × base × height. From three sides a, b, c: first the semiperimeter s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2, then Heron's formula, area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)). The two methods agree whenever the height matches the sides; they are independent checks on each other. The three sides must satisfy the triangle inequality — each side shorter than the sum of the other two — or no triangle exists.

Base 10 and height 6: area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30. For the 3–4–5 triangle: s = (3 + 4 + 5) ÷ 2 = 6, so area = √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = √36 = 6, and the perimeter is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. The 3–4–5 triangle is right-angled (3² + 4² = 5²), so its area also equals ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 — a third way to the same answer.

This page computes area only; it does not find missing sides or angles (a right triangle's sides and angles are covered by the right triangle calculator). Heron's formula needs all three sides and a valid triangle: if any side is zero or negative, or the triangle inequality fails, the page says so instead of showing a square root of a negative number. Results are in square units of whatever length unit you entered — the page does not convert units.
Why half of base times height?
Because a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height: two copies of the triangle make the parallelogram, whose area is base × height. Halving gives the triangle.
When do I use Heron's formula?
When you know three sides but no height — for example, a plot of land measured along its three boundaries. If you know a base and its height, the simpler formula is enough.
Half the perimeter: s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2. Heron discovered that the area depends only on s and how far each side falls short of it. For 3–4–5, s = 6, and the shortfalls are 3, 2, and 1.
What if the sides cannot form a triangle?
Then the triangle inequality fails — for example sides 1, 2, and 10, where 1 + 2 is less than 10. No such triangle exists, and the page reports that instead of a meaningless number.
Do the two methods always agree?

For a genuine triangle, yes, provided the height belongs to the base you entered. If base-height area and Heron area disagree, one of the inputs is inconsistent — usually a height measured to the wrong base.
Does this work for any triangle type?
Yes: acute, right, obtuse, isosceles, and equilateral all use the same two formulas. Equilateral triangles have a shortcut (area = √3 ÷ 4 × side²), but Heron's formula gives the same result.

Population and sample variance of a data set — with mean and both standard deviations alongside.
Population and sample variance of a data set — with the mean and both standard deviations alongside.
Enter at least two numbers. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

First the mean x̄ = (sum of values) ÷ n. Then the sum of squared deviations SS = Σ(x − x̄)². Population variance (when the data is the whole group) is SS ÷ n; sample variance (when the data is a sample from a larger group) is SS ÷ (n − 1). Standard deviation is the square root of variance, back in the original units. The n − 1 divisor (Bessel's correction) compensates for the fact that a sample's own mean sits closer to its points than the true mean does.

2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: the sum is 40 and n = 8, so the mean is 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, summing to SS = 32. Population variance = 32 ÷ 8 = 4.00 (SD 2.00); sample variance = 32 ÷ 7 = 4.57 (SD 2.14). The sample figure is larger because it divides by the smaller number — the standard adjustment when generalising from a sample to a population.

This page describes spread only; it says nothing about the shape of the distribution, outliers, or whether the mean is a good summary. Variance is in squared units (square dollars, square centimetres), which is why standard deviation is usually the reported figure — it returns to the original units. A single extreme value inflates variance a lot, so for skewed data consider the median and interquartile range alongside. Sample variance needs at least two values; with one value it is undefined.
Which variance do I use, population or sample?

Population when your data is everyone you care about (all employees, all products tested). Sample when your data is a subset meant to stand for a larger group (a survey, a trial batch). Most real-world analysis uses the sample version.
Why divide by n − 1 for a sample?

Because the sample mean is itself fitted to the data, the squared deviations around it are systematically a little too small. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n corrects that bias on average — Bessel's correction.
Why square the deviations at all?

Because plain deviations sum to zero by definition of the mean — positives cancel negatives. Squaring makes every deviation positive before averaging, and it also penalises large deviations more than small ones.
What is the difference between variance and standard deviation?

Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variance is the mathematically convenient quantity; standard deviation is the interpretable one, because it is back in the original units (dollars, centimetres, points).
Yes, when every value is identical — there is no spread at all. It can never be negative, since it is an average of squares.
Does variance tell me about outliers?
Indirectly: a large variance relative to the mean often signals outliers or a wide spread, but variance alone cannot identify them. Look at the sorted values and the range alongside.

Average speed = distance ÷ time. Metres per second = km/h ÷ 3.6. Pace per kilometre = 60 ÷ speed in km/h, in minutes per kilometre.
100 km in 2 hours: average speed = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 km/h. In metres per second that is 50 ÷ 3.6 = 13.89 m/s. Pace = 60 ÷ 50 = 1.20 minutes per kilometre — that is 1 minute 12 seconds per kilometre.

This is average speed over the whole trip: it says nothing about how fast you went at any one moment. Stops, traffic, and hills are all folded into the average. Direction is ignored — this is speed (a scalar), not velocity as a vector, even though the two share the name in everyday use. Time must be above zero; a zero time gives no meaningful speed.

Average: total distance over total time. Your speedometer shows instantaneous speed, which can be higher or lower at any moment. A trip with stops can have a high speedometer reading and a low average.
Because 1 km/h = 1,000 metres per 3,600 seconds, and 1,000 ÷ 3,600 = 1 ÷ 3.6. So 50 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 13.89 m/s.
What is pace, and why minutes per kilometre?
Pace is the inverse of speed: time per unit distance. Runners and walkers use it because "6 minutes per kilometre" is easier to hold steady than "10 km/h".
Can I enter miles and minutes?
Not directly here: convert first (1 mile = 1.60934 km, minutes ÷ 60 = hours). The speed converter on this site converts the result afterwards.
Does a round trip change anything?

No, if you enter total distance and total time. Note the trap: going 60 km/h out and 40 km/h back does not average to 50 km/h — the slower leg takes longer, so the true average over equal distances is 48 km/h.

Average acceleration, signed displacement and travelled distance from initial velocity, final velocity and elapsed time.

Average acceleration a = (v₁ − v₀) ÷ t. With constant acceleration, signed displacement is s = ((v₀ + v₁) ÷ 2) × t. If velocity reverses sign, travelled distance is the sum of the distances before and after the zero-velocity time, not the absolute displacement. Negative acceleration means signed velocity decreases; speed can increase or decrease depending on direction. Enter velocity in m/s and time in seconds for acceleration in m/s² and displacement or distance in metres.

This page computes average acceleration over the interval, assuming it is constant. Real acceleration usually varies (an engine's pull fades as speed rises), in which case this result is the average, not the peak. It is one-dimensional and supports reversal along that axis. Curved paths, circular motion and multi-axis vector components are not covered. Time must be above zero — an instant change (t = 0) would imply infinite acceleration, which the page refuses rather than displays.

Negative acceleration points along the negative axis. It reduces speed when velocity is positive, but increases speed when velocity is negative. If velocity crosses zero, the object slows, reverses direction, then speeds up.

CalcMintly provides 500 free calculators for everyday questions, technical checks and planning scenarios. No account is required.
Each tool has editable assumptions, a reproducible method, an example and limitations. The workspace brings up to four tools together; unit-compatible links are explicit and removable.

The default directory order is an editorial selection, not a measured global usage ranking. The three original scenario designs combine transparent time, dependency and commitment models; no claim of worldwide uniqueness is made.

The current calculators are free, with no checkout or account system. Advertising and behavioral analytics are not enabled. If commercial services are added, their terms and data practices will be disclosed before use.
Calculate average acceleration, signed displacement and travelled distance, including straight-line direction reversal.

Uses the proleptic Gregorian calendar and date-only arithmetic, independent of daylight saving time. Complete years and months use the original day of month, clamped to the last valid day when necessary. Other anniversary conventions can differ; this is not a legal age determination.

All prices are editable examples in USD per million tokens, not a current provider quote. Zero calls means zero monthly cost; the hypothetical cost per call still follows your token and price assumptions. Caching, reasoning tokens, discounts, other modalities, taxes and rate limits require separate entries or estimates.

For gross-revenue tax: revenue × (1 − tax rate) − expenses = income target. For profit-basis tax: (revenue − expenses) × (1 − tax rate) = income target. The selected basis is an assumption, not a tax ruling.
There is no retained-share floor. A tax rate of 100% is outside this model.

At the default gross-revenue tax basis: target 240,000 + expenses 30,000 = 270,000. Divide by 0.8 to get revenue 337,500. Billable hours = 40 × 48 × 0.6 = 1,152. Required rate = 337,500 / 1,152 = 292.96875 per hour.
Selecting profit-basis tax changes the same example to revenue 330,000 and a required rate of 286.458333333 per hour. This illustrates why the tax-basis assumption matters.

This is a planning model with one effective tax rate and an editable working-year assumption. It does not apply tax brackets, social contributions, deductions or local rules. Confirm which expenses, if any, reduce your actual taxable base.

Unpaid administration, marketing, leave and downtime must be reflected in your working weeks or billable share. A required rate is a break-even target for your assumptions, not a market-rate recommendation.
Why two tax bases? Expenses may or may not be deductible in your actual situation. The choice changes the arithmetic; it does not determine legal eligibility for deductions.
Why 48 weeks? It is an editable example allowing time off. Replace it with your own realistic working year.
What if billable time is zero? No finite hourly rate can cover a positive annual target without billable hours.

Ending wealth at the planning horizon

Both sides start with the same cash. The renter invests the down payment and purchase fees; whichever side spends less each month invests the difference. Values can be negative, even when a bar is clipped at zero.
Mortgage payments stop after the loan term. Home value, rent and alternative investments compound monthly from the annual assumptions; holding time rounds to the nearest month.
Investment contributions occur at month end. Growth is smooth in this scenario; real markets do not follow a constant path.

Default example: price 400,000; 30% down; 6.5% mortgage for 30 years; hold 10 years; rent 2,000; home and rent growth 2%; purchase fees 3%; sale fees 5%; annual ownership costs 1.5%; alternative return 5%.

Monthly mortgage is 1,769.79046578. The final mortgage balance is 237,373.15381644 and home value is 487,597.76799790. Owner ending wealth is 226,406.27374355; renter ending wealth is 234,962.36304386. The difference is −8,556.08930031, so renting has higher ending wealth in this example.

All prices, growth rates, costs and returns are editable assumptions, not market forecasts. The combined ownership rate represents the tax, insurance and maintenance you choose; do not add the same cost twice. The model excludes local tax deductions, rent deposits, moving costs, borrowing restrictions and individual investment taxes.

A larger ending wealth is one modeled financial comparison, not a recommendation to buy or rent. Test negative appreciation, lower investment returns, different horizons and realistic ownership costs.
Can the mortgage rate be zero? Yes. Payments become principal divided by the number of months, without dividing by a zero rate.
What happens after the mortgage ends? The remaining balance and mortgage payments become zero; the comparison continues with ongoing ownership costs and invested cash-flow differences.
Can home prices fall? Yes. Appreciation may be negative above −100%, and ending equity can be negative.

Why do the answers change with investment assumptions? Money tied up in a home and monthly cash-flow differences have an opportunity cost. The entered alternative return explicitly models that assumption.

First calculate a fixed monthly payment from the principal, nominal interest rate and whole number of months. Then find the monthly discount rate that makes the present value of all payments equal principal minus upfront fees. The displayed annualized rate is 12 times that monthly rate; the effective annual rate compounds it for a year. At zero interest with no fees, both rates are exactly zero.

For a $10,000 loan at 6% nominal interest over 36 months with $300 upfront fees, the unrounded monthly payment is about $304.21937452. Total payments round to $10,951.90 and proceeds are $9,700. The discount rate gives an annualized rate of about 8.06% and an effective annual rate of about 8.36%. Calculations use unrounded payments; actual payment rounding can change the result.

This is a mathematical fixed-payment loan cost model with equally spaced monthly payments and fees deducted at the start. It is not a jurisdiction-specific statutory APR disclosure. Local rules determine included charges, timing, rounding and disclosure conventions. Variable rates, irregular dates, optional services and later charges are not modeled. Compare lender disclosures using the rules and cash flows that apply to that loan.
What is the difference between the two annual rates?

The annualized rate multiplies the monthly discount rate by 12. The effective annual rate compounds it over a year. Both describe this model; neither label guarantees that a lender or local law uses the same calculation.

The monthly discount rate equals the entered nominal annual rate divided by 12. With a positive rate, annual compounding produces a higher effective rate. At zero interest and zero fees, both rates are zero.
Can I use a zero-interest loan with an upfront fee?
Yes. Payments still repay the principal, but the fee reduces the amount received, producing a positive discount rate and borrowing cost.

Monthly fee 68, 2 uses per active month, alternative price 12 per use and 4 idle months: annual fee = 68 × 12 = 816; active months = 12 − 4 = 8; alternative cost = 2 × 8 × 12 = 192; difference = 816 − 192 = 624. Idle fees of 4 × 68 = 272 are already inside the annual fee. These are fictional example prices.

The difference is a comparison with paying per use, not guaranteed cash recovered by cancelling.

For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂, D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁. If D ≠ 0, x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁) ÷ D and y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁) ÷ D. If D = 0, consistent dependent constraints have infinitely many solutions; contradictory constraints have none. An equation with zero coefficients and a nonzero constant is a contradiction.

This page solves two linear equations in two unknowns, including identity and contradictory zero-coefficient rows. It does not solve nonlinear terms, inequalities or larger systems. A non-degenerate linear equation describes a line. Two intersecting lines give one solution; distinct parallel lines give none; coincident lines give infinitely many. A zero-coefficient equation instead describes either no restriction or a contradiction.

x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] ÷ 2a. The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the root type: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, D < 0 gives two complex roots. The vertex (turning point) sits at x = −b ÷ 2a.
It is the parabola's turning point: the minimum when a > 0, the maximum when a < 0. It sits exactly halfway between the two real roots when they exist.
A polynomial of degree 2 has two roots counting multiplicity. They can coincide (one repeated root) or be a complex pair, but there are always two.

Uniform independent hashes only. Up to 10,000 hashes use the no-collision product in log space; larger counts use the birthday approximation. More hashes than possible outputs guarantee a collision. This is not a cryptographic security proof or a model of adversarial collisions.
n is the hash count and b is the width in bits. For n ≤ 10,000, P = 1 − ∏(1 − k/2^b), k = 0…n−1. Larger counts use P ≈ 1 − exp[−n(n−1)/(2×2^b)]. If n > 2^b, P = 1.
