Use q ≤ min(R/60,c/s) and t ≈ N/q. R is requests allowed per minute, c is concurrent slots, s is average service seconds, N is batch requests, q is requests per second, and t is ideal batch seconds.
Reduce W:H by dividing both dimensions by gcd(W,H). For a new width w, the proportional height is h = wH/W. gcd is the greatest common divisor.
Use S = bt/8000. b is the audio bitrate in kbps, t is duration in seconds, and S is decimal MB.
Use v = 8000Gc/(3600hη). G is source GB, c is the compressed-size fraction, h is available hours, η is efficiency, and v is required Mbps.
Use C = Gr+Nq/10^6+Ep. G is stored GB-months, r is storage price, N is requests, q is price per million requests, E is egress GB, and p is egress price per GB.
For a series system use A = ∏Aᵢ. For ideal parallel redundancy use A = 1−∏(1−Aᵢ). Each Aᵢ is an independent component availability as a fraction.
Use A = W−S−H−O. W is context capacity, S is system and tool tokens, H is existing history, O is reserved output, and A is remaining input capacity. All terms are token counts.
Use t = 8000G/(vη). G is the file size in decimal GB, v is the link speed in Mbps, η is the efficiency fraction, and t is seconds.
Use m = 100(f₁−f₀)/(v₁−v₀) and b = f₀−mv₀/100. The fluid size is clamp(f₀, b + m×vw, f₁); f denotes font sizes and v denotes viewport widths.
Use B = 2^(32−p) and N = floor(A/B)×B. p is the prefix length, A is the integer address, B is the address block size, and N is the network address.
Use S = 2^(c−p) and A = 2^(128−c). p is the parent prefix, c is the child prefix, S is the number of child subnets, and A is addresses per child subnet.
Use T = Σtᵢ and R = B−T. Each tᵢ is a sequential stage duration, B is the target, T is total latency, and R is the remaining budget.
For each dimension, use c = p×2.54/PPI. p is the pixel count, c is centimetres, and PPI is pixels per inch.
Use PPI = √(W²+H²)/d. W and H are pixel dimensions and d is the screen diagonal in inches.
Use H = L×log₂(A). L is the independently sampled password length, A is the alphabet size, and H is entropy in bits.
Use t ≈ 2^(b−1)/g. b is search-space entropy in bits, g is assumed guesses per second, and t is expected search time in seconds.
Use C = Nhr+Gp+F. N is instance count, h is hours per instance, r is hourly price, G is billable traffic GB, p is price per GB, and F is fixed charges.
Use d = T(1−a). T is the reporting-period duration, a is availability as a fraction, and d is allowed downtime in the same time unit.
Use D = 1000T(1−r)/(gc). T is capacity in decimal TB, r is the reserve fraction, g is new GB per day, c is the copy count, and D is retention days.
Use B = ceil(WHd/8). W and H are pixel dimensions, d is bits per pixel, B is bytes, and ceil rounds up to a whole byte.
Use S = (v+a/1000)t(1+h)/8. v is video Mbps, a is audio kbps, t is duration in seconds, h is the overhead fraction, and S is decimal MB.
Use P = A×a(r,n). A is the monthly payment budget, r is the monthly interest fraction, and n is months. a(r,n) is the sum of end-of-month discount factors. The result is payment arithmetic only.
Use U = Σ(Aᵢ/Pᵢ) and P̄ = (ΣAᵢ+F)/U. Aᵢ is each purchase amount excluding fees, Pᵢ is its unit price, F is total fees, and U is total units bought. P̄ includes fees.

Use A = [P−B/(1+r)^n]/a(r,n). P is principal, B is the balloon balance, r is the monthly interest fraction, and n is months. a(r,n) sums the end-of-month discount factors; the balloon is paid at the end.

Use K = Σ[k(k+1)CFₖ/(1+y/m)^(k+2)]/(Pm²). CFₖ is the payment in coupon period k, P is bond price, y is the nominal annual yield fraction, and m is payments per year. K estimates local price curvature with respect to yield.

Use PVₖ = CFₖ/(1+y/m)^k, tₖ = k/m, D = Σ(tₖPVₖ)/P and Dₘ = D/(1+y/m). CFₖ is the payment in coupon period k, including principal when due; m is payments per year, y is the annual yield fraction, and P is the sum of discounted payments. Both durations are in years.

Solve P = Σ C/(1+y/m)^k + F/(1+y/m)^N for y. P is market price, F is face value, C is each coupon payment, m is payments per year, and N is total coupon periods. y is the nominal annual yield fraction.

Use G = S−F−B and T = max(G,0)r. S is sale proceeds, F is sale fees, B is purchase cost basis, and r is the entered gains tax fraction. G is modeled gain and T is estimated tax; no jurisdiction rules are applied.
Use CCC = DIO+DSO−DPO. DIO is inventory days, DSO is receivable days, and DPO is payable days. The result is the modeled cash conversion cycle in days.
Use C = P−V, M = C/P and T = QC. P is unit price, V is unit variable cost, and Q is units sold. C is contribution per unit, M is the contribution fraction, and T is total contribution.
Use Y = C/P. C is annual coupon income, P is the purchase price, and Y is current yield as a fraction. This ratio excludes capital gains and time to maturity.
Use R = A/L. A is current assets and L is current liabilities. The current ratio is a dimensionless comparison of those entered amounts.
Use CAC = A/N. A is the acquisition spending attributed to the same period and customer group, and N is the number of newly acquired paying customers.
Use c = L/S and r = 1−c. S is starting customers and L is customers lost from that starting group. c is the churn fraction and r is the retained fraction; new customers do not enter either numerator.

Use LTV = Rm/c−S. R is monthly revenue per customer, m is the contribution-margin fraction, c is the monthly churn fraction, and S is one-time servicing cost. Constant churn gives an expected lifetime of 1/c months; this model does not discount future contributions.
Use Y = D/P. D is annual dividend per share, P is share price, and Y is dividend yield as a fraction. Price changes and dividend reinvestment are excluded.
Use EPS = (E−D)/S. E is net earnings, D is preferred dividends, and S is weighted average common shares. This is basic earnings per share.
Use EOQ = √(2DS/H). D is annual demand in units, S is cost per order, and H is annual holding cost per unit. The result balances modeled ordering and holding costs.
Use EAR = (1+j/m)^m−1. j is the nominal annual rate as a fraction, m is compounding periods per year, and EAR is the effective annual rate as a fraction.

Use EAC = [P−S/(1+r)^n]/a(r,n)+C. P is purchase cost, S is final resale value, C is annual operating cost, r is the annual discount fraction, and n is years. a(r,n) is the sum of the end-of-year discount factors.

Flat interest is I = Pjn/12; reducing-balance payment is A = P/a(j/12,n). P is principal, j is the nominal annual interest fraction, and n is months. a(r,n) sums the monthly discount factors at rate r.
Use IR = (R−B)/e. R is portfolio return, B is benchmark return, and e is tracking error. All inputs must refer to the same period and rate units.
Monthly interest is I = Pr/12 and term interest is nI. P is principal, r is the nominal annual interest fraction, and n is months. Interest-only payments leave the principal due.

Find a supported r satisfying Σ Cₜ/(1+r)^t = 0. Cₜ is the equally spaced cash flow at period t, starting at time zero. r is the return per cash-flow period; a cash-flow series can have no root or multiple roots.
Use SS = zσ√L. z is the chosen service factor, σ is the standard deviation of daily demand, and L is fixed lead time in days. Daily demand is assumed independent with stable variance.
Use T = C/I and D = d/T. C is cost of goods sold for the period, I is average inventory, and d is days in that period. T is turnover and D is inventory days.
Use t = ln(M)/ln(1+r). M is the target growth multiple, r is the annual effective growth fraction, and t is years. This generalizes doubling to the multiple you enter.

Use A = [(C−S)/n+(C+S)f](1+τ). C is adjusted capitalized cost, S is residual value, n is months, f is the money factor, and τ is the payment tax fraction. The two terms are depreciation and financing charges.
At each time, compare portfolio value with the highest value reached so far. The drawdown is 1−Vₜ/Hₜ; maximum drawdown is the largest such fraction. Vₜ is current value and Hₜ is the running peak.

Use MIRR = (F/abs(P))^(1/n)−1. F is positive cash flows accumulated to the final period at the reinvestment rate, P is negative cash flows discounted to time zero at the financing rate, and n is the number of intervals. abs means absolute value.
Use NPV = Σ Cₜ/(1+r)^t, including the cash flow at time zero. Cₜ is cash flow at period t and r is the discount rate per period as a fraction. Cash flows use equal time intervals.

Use NRR = (S+E−D−C)/S. S is starting recurring revenue, E is expansion, D is contraction, and C is churned revenue from the same starting customer group. NRR is a fraction; all new-customer revenue is excluded.
Use j = m[(1+EAR)^(1/m)−1]. EAR is the effective annual rate as a fraction, m is compounding periods per year, and j is the equivalent nominal annual rate as a fraction.
Use DOL = Q(P−V)/[Q(P−V)−F]. Q is units sold, P is selling price per unit, V is variable cost per unit, and F is fixed operating costs. The denominator is modeled operating profit.
Use T = S/A and D = d/T. S is net credit purchases, A is average trade payables, and d is days in the same period. T is payables turnover and D is payment days.
Use PB = P/B. P is share price and B is book value per share. The ratio compares share price with the entered book value.
Use PE = P/E. P is share price and E is annual earnings per share. The ratio compares share price with the entered annual earnings.

Use PI = Σ Cₜ/(1+r)^t / I for periods after the initial investment. Cₜ is a future inflow, r is the discount rate per period as a fraction, and I is the initial cost. The ratio compares discounted inflows with that cost.
Use Q = (A−I−P)/L. A is current assets, I is inventory, P is prepayments, and L is current liabilities. The quick ratio excludes inventory and prepayments from the numerator.
With N equal-size disks of S TB, usable capacity is NS for RAID0, S for RAID1, (N−1)S for RAID5, (N−2)S for RAID6, and NS/2 for RAID10. Redundancy does not replace a backup.
Use R = (1+r)/(1+f)−1. r is nominal return, f is inflation, and R is real return. Rates in the equation are fractions over the same period.
Use T = S/A and D = d/T. S is net credit sales, A is average receivables, and d is days in the same period. T is receivables turnover and D is collection days.
Use ROP = dL+S. d is average daily demand, L is lead time in days, and S is safety stock. The reorder point combines lead-time demand with that stock allowance.
Use ROAS = R/A and break-even ROAS = 1/m. R is attributed revenue, A is advertising spend, and m is the pre-ad contribution-margin fraction. Modeled contribution after advertising is Rm−A.
The rule gives t ≈ 72/p, while constant compound growth gives t = ln(2)/ln(1+p/100). p is the positive annual percentage rate and t is years. The rule is an approximation.
Use S = (R−F)/σ. R is period return, F is the risk-free return, and σ is volatility. All three inputs must use the same period and consistent rate units.
Use S = (R−T)/d. R is period return, T is the same-period target return, and d is downside deviation measured consistently with that target and period.

Use P = C/(1−m−f). C is unit cost including fixed per-sale fees, m is the target profit-margin fraction, and f is the revenue-based fee fraction. The combined fractions must leave a positive denominator.
Use T = (R−F)/β. R and F are the period return and same-period risk-free return as fractions; β is the entered positive market beta. The result uses decimal return per unit of beta.
Use WACC = E×rₑ/(D+E)+D×r_d×(1−τ)/(D+E). E and D are equity and debt market values. rₑ, r_d and τ are equity cost, debt cost and effective tax rate, each as a fraction.
Use NWC = A−L. A is current assets and L is current liabilities. Dividing NWC by the entered annual revenue gives the working-capital-to-revenue fraction.
Use ACH = Q/V. Q is measured airflow in m³/h and V is room volume in m³. ACH is air changes per hour; it is a flow-to-volume ratio, not a contaminant-removal guarantee.
Use G = Va×0.789. V is drink volume in mL and a is alcohol by volume as a fraction. G is estimated ethanol mass in g. Divide by your entered grams per standard drink for standard-drink equivalents.
Use S = (Eₒ−Eₙ)p. Eₒ and Eₙ are old and new annual energy use in kWh, and p is price per kWh. S is annual bill saving; simple payback divides net replacement cost by a positive saving.
Use M = Adρ(1+w). A is area in m², d is compacted thickness converted to m, ρ is density in kg/m³, and w is the waste fraction. M is kilograms before conversion to tonnes.

Use Fₚ = S/(1+h), Wₚ = S−Fₚ and H = (W+Wₚ)/(F+Fₚ). S is preferment mass, h is its hydration fraction, and F and W are main-dough flour and water, all masses in g. Total hydration H is displayed as a percentage.
Use B = twLq/12. t and w are thickness and width in in, L is length in ft, and q is piece count. B is total board feet.
Use BSA = √(HW/3600). H is height in cm and W is body mass in kg. The Mosteller estimate is in m².
Use N = ceil[(A−O)(1+w)/((l+j)(h+j))]. A and O are wall and opening areas in m²; brick face dimensions l, h and joint width j are converted to m. w is the waste fraction and ceil rounds up.
Use W = Cr. C is coffee mass in g and r is water grams per gram of coffee. W is required water mass in g; the ratio compares water with coffee.
Use v = c(F/R)C×0.06. c is cadence in revolutions per minute, F and R are front and rear tooth counts, and C is loaded wheel circumference in m. Speed v is in km/h.
Use R = P/m. P is measured power in W and m is body mass in kg. Relative power is in W/kg.

Use N = ceil[(W+g)/(b+g)]. W is deck width, b is board width, and g is the gap, all in the same unit. ceil rounds up to board rows. Stock board count also accounts for length without reusing cut pieces.

Use S = (fp−eq)D/100. f is fuel litres and e is EV wall energy in kWh per 100 km; p is fuel price per litre, q is electricity price per kWh, and D is annual distance in km. S is annual energy-cost saving.

Estimate L = A−B+D−U and R = L/t. A and B are pre- and post-exercise mass in kg; D and U are drink and urine volumes in L; t is hours. The approximation treats a kilogram of mass change as a litre of fluid; R is in L/h.
Use FFMI = W(1−f)/h². W is body mass in kg, f is measured body fat as a fraction, and h is height converted to m. The index is in kg/m².
Use FMI = Wf/h². W is body mass in kg, f is measured body fat as a fraction, and h is height converted to m. The index is in kg/m².
Let n = ceil(L/s), where L is fence length and s is maximum post spacing in the same unit. Open-run post count is n+1; a closed loop uses n posts. ceil rounds up.
Use M = An/f. A is area in m², n is the separately confirmed nitrogen target in g/m², and f is product nitrogen by mass as a fraction. M is product grams before conversion to kilograms.
Use N = ceil[A(1+w)/C]. A is net area and C is coverage per pack in the same area unit. w is the waste fraction. ceil rounds up to whole packs.
Use d = E/W and Q = ds. E is measured-portion energy in kcal, W is its mass in g, and s is target serving mass in g. d is energy per gram and Q is target serving energy in kcal.
Use M = Ar(1+w). A is area in m², r is labelled sowing rate in g/m², and w is the waste fraction. M is grams before conversion to kilograms; packs are rounded up using entered pack mass.
Use V = Ad(1+c). A is area in m², d is finished depth converted to m, and c is the extra loose-volume fraction for compaction. Loose volume V is in m³.
Use T = R+(M−R)i. R is resting heart rate, M is measured maximum heart rate, and i is your chosen reserve intensity as a fraction. T uses the same heart-rate unit.
Use A = r²acos((r−h)/r)−(r−h)√(2rh−h²) and V = AL. r is inner radius, h is liquid depth from the bottom, and L is cylinder length, all in m. acos uses radians; V is in m³.
Use E = A(Uₒ−Uₙ)D×24/(1000η). A is area in m²; Uₒ and Uₙ are old and new transmittance in W/m²·K; D is annual heating degree days in K·day; η is system efficiency. E is annual energy saving in kWh.
Use V = Ad/e and t = V/q. A is area in m², d is chosen water depth in mm, e is application efficiency as a fraction, and q is total emitter flow in L/min. V is litres and t is minutes.

Use N = floor[(L+k)/(p+k)]. L is stock length, p is finished piece length, and k is saw kerf in the same unit. floor rounds down. This counts kerf between pieces; a final separation cut may need another kerf.
Use E = 4P+4C+9F. P, C and F are grams of protein, available carbohydrate and fat. Estimated energy E is in kcal, using general food-label factors.
Use I = 100H/M. H is observed heart rate and M is the entered measured maximum, in the same unit. I is the percentage of that maximum.
Use V = 10Ad and N = ceil(V/B). A is area in m², d is depth in cm, and B is litres per bag. V is litres and ceil rounds up to whole bags.
For r > 1, use Epley E = w(1+r/30); at r = 1 use E = w. Brzycki uses B = 36w/(37−r). w is lifted weight and r is completed repetitions. Both results use the weight unit.
Use V = lw(a+b)/2. l and w are rectangular pool length and width; a and b are shallow and deep depths, all in m. V is in m³, assuming a uniformly sloping floor.

Use V = Are. A is roof catchment area in m², r is rainfall in mm, and e is collection efficiency as a fraction. V is potential collected litres; actual storage is capped by entered spare tank capacity.
Use g = h/l and s = √(h²+l²). h is rise and l is horizontal run in the same unit. Gradient g is displayed as a percentage; ramp length s keeps the distance unit.
Use q = xB/A. x is an original ingredient amount, A is original servings, and B is target servings. Each scaled amount q retains that ingredient's original unit.

Use θ = atan(r/l) and S = A√(1+(r/l)²). r is roof rise and l is horizontal run in the same unit. A is horizontal projected area and S is sloping area in the same area unit. The angle is displayed in degrees.
Use N = ceil(AE/(Φum)). A is area in m², E is chosen illuminance in lux, Φ is lumens per fixture, and u and m are utilization and maintenance factors. ceil rounds up to whole fixtures.
Use T = n(r+w) and D = n(ra+wb)/60. n is cycles; r and w are running and walking minutes per cycle. a and b are the corresponding speeds in km/h. T is minutes and D is km.
Use v = cs×0.06. c is cadence in steps per minute and s is the length of a single step in m. Speed v is in km/h.
Use t = Ts/D. T is total finish time in minutes, s is split length, and D is total distance in the same distance unit. t is full-split time in minutes under an even-pace assumption.
Use L = tR. t is session duration in minutes and R is the entered session rating of perceived exertion. L is a load score in arbitrary units, not energy expenditure.
Use E = (B−L−W)/B. B is time in bed, L is sleep-onset latency, and W is later awake time, all in minutes. Sleep efficiency E is a fraction, displayed as a percentage.
Use E = Ph(1−l)d. P is peak array capacity in kW, h is average peak sun hours per day, l is system loss as a fraction, and d is days. Period energy E is in kWh.
Use N = ceil(H/r) and T = N−1. H is total rise and r is the preferred maximum riser height in the same unit. ceil rounds up; T counts treads before the upper landing. Actual riser height is H/N.
Use S = L/W. L is lifted load and W is body mass in the same weight unit. The result is the load as a multiple of body mass.
Use P = 100t/d. t is elapsed time in minutes and d is distance in m. P is minutes per 100 m. Pool lengths equal distance divided by pool length.

Use f = 1−lb/[(l+j)(b+j)] and V = Afd. l, b and j are tile length, width and joint width in the same unit; A is area in m² and d is joint depth in mm. V is litres; mass also includes entered density and waste.
Use N = ceil[A(1+w)/(lb)]. A is net area in m², l and b are tile dimensions converted to m, and w is waste allowance as a fraction. ceil rounds up to whole tiles; boxes are rounded up separately.

Use M = μ/σ and S = LM. μ is mean daily load, σ is population standard deviation of the seven entered daily loads, and L is their sum. Monotony M and strain S are undefined when daily variation is zero.
Use T = D/v+s/60. D is distance in km, v is average moving speed in km/h, and s is total stop time in minutes. Total travel time T is in hours.

Use B = (T+nH+pdF)(1+w). T is group transport cost, n is nights, H is group lodging cost per night, p is people, d is days, F is daily spending per person, and w is the buffer fraction. Costs use the same currency.
Use R = W/H. W is measured waist circumference and H is measured height in the same unit. The ratio has no unit.
Use WHR = W/H. W is waist circumference and H is hip circumference, measured in the same unit.
Use N = ceil(L/s)+1. L is wall length and s is maximum centre spacing, converted to the same unit. ceil rounds up the number of intervals; the extra position includes both ends.
Use A = abs(x). x is the entered real number and abs means its distance from zero. The absolute value is nonnegative; the separate sign result identifies positive, negative or zero input.
Use θ = acos[(A·B)/(norm(A)norm(B))]. A and B are nonzero vectors, the dot denotes their dot product, and norm means Euclidean magnitude. The angle is displayed in degrees.
Use ω = 2πn/60 and v = ωr. n is rotations per minute and r is radius in m. Angular speed ω is in rad/s and tangential speed v is in m/s.
Use A = π(R²−r²) and P = 2π(R+r). R and r are outer and inner radii in the same unit. A is annular area; P includes both boundary circles.
Use θ = s/r and c = 2r sin(θ/2). s is arc length and r is radius in the same unit. θ is radians before conversion to displayed degrees; c is chord length.
Use t = VCfη/P. V is nominal voltage in V, C is capacity in Ah, f is usable discharge fraction, η is conversion efficiency as a fraction, and P is constant load in W. Runtime t is in hours.

In (ax+b)^n, the coefficient of x^(n−k) is C(n,k)a^(n−k)b^k. a and b are entered constants, n is the nonnegative integer power, and k runs from zero through that power. C(n,k) is a binomial coefficient.
Use P = 1−∏ᵢ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(1−i/d). n is people and d is equally likely days; the product is the no-match probability. If people outnumber days, a match is certain. The result assumes independent birthdays.
Use F = ρVg. ρ is fluid density in kg/m³, V is displaced fluid volume in m³, and g is gravity in m/s². Buoyant force F is in N.
Use η = 1−T_c/T_h. T_c and T_h are cold and hot reservoir absolute temperatures in K. The theoretical efficiency fraction η is displayed as a percentage; the hot reservoir must be hotter.
Use χ² = Σ(Oᵢ−Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ and df = k−1−p. Oᵢ and Eᵢ are observed and expected counts, k is category count, and p is parameters estimated from the same data. The p-value is the upper chi-square tail.
Use c = 2√(r²−d²). r is radius and d is perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord in the same unit. Chord length c uses that length unit.
Convert the entered angle a in degrees to θ = πa/180 radians. Use A = r²(θ−sinθ)/2 and c = 2r sin(θ/2). r is radius, A is segment area, and c is chord length.
Use CV = 100s/μ. s is sample standard deviation and μ is the positive arithmetic mean of the entered nonnegative observations. The coefficient of variation is displayed as a percentage.
Use L = 10log₁₀[Σ10^(Lᵢ/10)]. Lᵢ are independent incoherent levels in dB, sharing the same reference, weighting and location. The combined level L uses the same basis.
Use P = hAΔT. h is convection coefficient in W/m²·K, A is surface area in m², and ΔT is signed surface-minus-fluid temperature difference in K. Heat flow rate P is in W.

Use tanh[atanh(r)±z/√(n−3)]. r is sample Pearson correlation, n is paired observation count, and z is the two-sided standard-normal critical value for the chosen confidence. The transforms convert between correlation and Fisher's scale.
Use θ = asin(n₂/n₁). n₁ is incident refractive index and n₂ is transmitted refractive index, with n₁ > n₂. The critical angle is measured from the normal and displayed in degrees.
Use V = lwh and S = 2(lw+lh+wh). l, w and h are cuboid length, width and height in the same unit. V is volume and S is total surface area.
Use Iₐ = IRᵦ/(Rₐ+Rᵦ) and Iᵦ = IRₐ/(Rₐ+Rᵦ). I is total current. Rₐ and Rᵦ are the parallel branch resistances in the same unit; each current result uses the input current unit.
Use R = max(x)−min(x). x is the entered observation list; max and min select its largest and smallest values. The range R uses the observations' unit.
Use d sinθ = mλ. d is slit spacing, λ is wavelength converted to the same length unit, and m is diffraction order. The angle is displayed in degrees; an order beyond the real-angle range is rejected.

Use fₒ = fₛ(c+vₒ)/(c−vₛ). fₛ is emitted frequency, c is sound speed in the medium, vₒ is observer velocity toward the source, and vₛ is source velocity toward the observer. Velocities share a unit; both moving speeds must be subsonic.
Use F = ρv²C_dA/2. ρ is fluid density in kg/m³, v is relative speed in m/s, C_d is the entered drag coefficient, and A is reference frontal area in m². Drag magnitude F is in N.

Use vₐ = [(mₐ−mᵦ)uₐ+2mᵦuᵦ]/(mₐ+mᵦ) and vᵦ = [2mₐuₐ+(mᵦ−mₐ)uᵦ]/(mₐ+mᵦ). m denotes mass, u initial signed velocity, and v final signed velocity; subscripts distinguish the bodies. Use consistent mass and velocity units.
Use P = VI and E = Pt/1000. V is voltage in V, I is current in A, and t is operating hours. Power P is in W and consumed energy E is in kWh.
Use V = 4πabc/3. a, b and c are the ellipsoid semiaxes in the same unit, not full diameters. Volume V uses the cubed length unit.

Use L = B⁻¹(α/2;k,n−k+1) and U = B⁻¹(1−α/2;k+1,n−k). k is successes, n is trials, α is one minus confidence, and B⁻¹ is the beta quantile. At no successes the lower bound is zero; at all successes the upper bound is unity.
Use μ = Σpᵢxᵢ and V = Σpᵢ(xᵢ−μ)². xᵢ are outcome values and pᵢ are matching probability fractions totaling unity. μ is expected value and V is variance; standard deviation is its square root.
Use y = b^e. b is the real base and e is the entered exponent. This tool requires an integer exponent for a negative base and a positive exponent for a zero base.
Use t = √(2h/g) and v = √(2gh). h is release height in m and g is gravity in m/s². Time t is in s and speed v is in m/s, starting from rest without air resistance.

Use S = max(a,e,c+n). a is start month, e is earliest stop month, c is cancellation-request month, and n is notice months. If S is within the item's end month, charge active months before it and the exit fee in the stop month; otherwise the original end remains.
Use G = exp[Σln(xᵢ)/n]. xᵢ are positive observations, n is their count, ln is natural logarithm, and exp is its inverse. Geometric mean G has the observations' unit.
Use V = 2πr³/3, C = 2πr² and S = 3πr². r is radius, V is hemisphere volume, C is curved area, and S includes the circular base.
Use P = Pₛ+ρgh. Pₛ is absolute surface pressure in Pa, ρ is fluid density in kg/m³, g is gravity in m/s², and h is depth in m. Absolute pressure P is in Pa.
Use sinh(x) = (e^x−e^(−x))/2, cosh(x) = (e^x+e^(−x))/2 and tanh(x) = sinh(x)/cosh(x). x is the real argument and e is Euler's number.
Use ρ = PM/(RT). P is absolute pressure in Pa, M is molar mass converted to kg/mol, T is absolute temperature in K, and R is the gas constant. Density ρ is in kg/m³.
Use P = nRT/V with R = 8.31446261815324 J/(mol·K). n is amount in mol, T is absolute temperature in K, and V is volume in m³. Pressure P is in Pa.
Use J = FΔt. F is average signed force in N and Δt is duration in s. Impulse J has units N·s and equals the modeled signed change in momentum.

For independent events, use P = ∏pᵢ for all events occurring and 1−P for not all occurring. pᵢ are entered probability fractions. The complement means at least one event fails, not that every event fails.
Use q = trunc(a/b) and r = a−bq. a is dividend and b is nonzero divisor. trunc rounds toward zero; q is quotient and r is the signed remainder.
Use IQR = Q₃−Q₁ with fences Q₁−1.5IQR and Q₃+1.5IQR. Q₁ and Q₃ are lower and upper quartiles using linear interpolation. Values beyond the fences are flagged, not automatically treated as errors.
Use a² = b²+c²−2bc cos(A) and K = bc sin(A)/2. b and c are the entered sides and A is their included angle in degrees. a is the opposite side and K is triangle area.
Use a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) and C = 180°−A−B. Each lowercase side is opposite its matching uppercase angle. Input angles are in degrees and side lengths share a unit.
Use lcm(a,b) = abs(ab)/gcd(a,b) repeatedly across the entered nonzero integers. gcd is greatest common divisor and abs means absolute value. The result is the least positive common multiple.

For an affected downstream resource, use dᵢ = max(dⱼ)+rᵢ over its dependencies. d is interruption hours and r is restart delay; the initial failure uses direct repair time. A backup can shorten one interruption. Total modeled loss is L = Σ(ℓᵢdᵢ)+B, where ℓ is independent hourly loss and B is activated backup cost.
Use b = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² and a = ȳ−bx̄. xᵢ and yᵢ are paired observations, bars denote means, b is slope, and a is intercept. Prediction at the entered target is a+bx.
Use log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b). x is a positive value and b is a positive base other than unity. ln is the natural logarithm.

Use F = abs(q)vB sinθ. q is charge converted from µC to C, v is speed in m/s, B is magnetic flux density in T, and θ is the velocity-field angle in degrees. abs means absolute value; force magnitude is in N.
For matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], use det = ad−bc. The letters give entries in row order. A zero determinant identifies a singular matrix.
For the matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], use λ = (a+d±√((a−d)²+4bc))/2. A negative discriminant gives conjugate complex eigenvalues; the result lists real and imaginary parts separately.
Use D = Σabs(xᵢ−μ)/n. xᵢ are observations, μ is their arithmetic mean, n is count, and abs means absolute value. D measures mean absolute distance from the mean.
Use m±t_c s/√n. m is sample mean, s is sample standard deviation, n is sample size, and t_c is the two-sided Student critical value for the chosen confidence and n−1 degrees of freedom.
Use W = Fs cosθ. F is force magnitude in N, s is displacement magnitude in m, and θ is the angle between them in degrees. Signed work W is in J.

Use D = median(abs(xᵢ−median(x))) and scaled value 1.482602218505602D. xᵢ are observations, median selects the middle of sorted values, and abs means absolute value. Scaling gives a normal-consistent spread estimate.
Use s(wd+n)/d. w is the whole part, n is fractional numerator, d is denominator, and s is the selected sign. The resulting fraction is reduced by its greatest common divisor.

Use T = (mₐcₐTₐ+mᵦcᵦTᵦ)/(mₐcₐ+mᵦcᵦ). m denotes mass, c specific heat, and subscripts identify the materials. Tₐ and Tᵦ are initial temperatures in °C; equilibrium temperature T uses the same scale. Assume no heat loss or phase change.
Use r = sign(x)abs(x)^(1/n). x is the radicand, n is a positive integer root degree, abs means absolute value, and sign gives the sign of the input. Negative inputs require an odd root degree.

Use OR = ad/(bc) and bounds exp[ln(OR)±1.96√(1/a+1/b+1/c+1/d)]. a and b are group A event and non-event counts; c and d are group B counts. The logarithmic interval uses a normal approximation and requires positive counts.
Use t = (m−μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n−1. m is sample mean, μ₀ is the null-hypothesis mean, s is sample standard deviation, and n is sample size. The displayed p-value is two-sided.
Use Cₑ = ΣCᵢ. Each Cᵢ is a positive parallel capacitance in µF. Sum all entered values for equivalent capacitance Cₑ in the same unit.
Use Rₑ = 1/Σ(1/Rᵢ). Each Rᵢ is a positive parallel resistor value in Ω. Sum their reciprocals, then take the reciprocal again for equivalent resistance Rₑ.
Use A = bh and P = 2(b+s). b is base, h is perpendicular height, and s is the adjacent side, all in the same length unit. A is area and P is perimeter.
Use E = 100abs(m−r)/abs(r). m is measured value, r is the nonzero reference in the same unit, and abs means absolute value. E is percent error.
Use R = 100(B+wE)/n. B counts observations below the target, E counts equal observations, and n is sample count. Convention weight w is 0 for strictly below, 0.5 for midrank, or 1 for inclusive rank.

Each week, update cash with C = C+I−E−A−U and free hours with H = T−F−P. I is income, E is essential spending, A is active-plan recurring costs, and U is newly starting plans' upfront costs. T is available hours, F is fixed hours, and P is active-plan hours.
Use d = abs(Ax+By+C)/√(A²+B²) for the line Ax+By+C = 0 and point (x,y). abs means absolute value. The line coefficients A and B cannot both be zero.
Use r = √(x²+y²) and θ = atan2(y,x). x and y are Cartesian coordinates in the same unit. Radius r keeps that unit; the signed angle θ is converted from radians to degrees for display.
Use A = abs[Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁−xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)]/2. (xᵢ,yᵢ) are vertices in boundary order; the last vertex connects back to the first. abs means absolute value. Coordinates must use the same length unit.

Integrate each polynomial term with ∫ aₙxⁿ dx = aₙx^(n+1)/(n+1), then evaluate F(b)−F(a). aₙ is a coefficient, n is its nonnegative integer power, and a and b are lower and upper limits. F is the summed antiderivative.

Use R = v²sin(2θ)/g and t = 2v sinθ/g. v is launch speed in m/s, θ is elevation in degrees, and g is gravity in m/s². Range R is in m and flight time t is in s, with equal launch and landing heights and no air resistance.

Use Wilson centre C = (p+z²/(2n))/(1+z²/n) and half-width H = z√[p(1−p)/n+z²/(4n²)]/(1+z²/n). p is successes divided by trials, n is trials, and z is the two-sided standard-normal critical value. Bounds are C−H and C+H, displayed as percentages.

Use y = Σ yᵢ ∏ⱼ≠ᵢ (x−xⱼ)/(xᵢ−xⱼ) over the three entered points (xᵢ,yᵢ). x is the target coordinate. The input horizontal coordinates must be distinct; outside them, the polynomial is an extrapolation.

Use R² = 1−SSE/SST and RMSE = √(SSE/n). SSE is summed squared prediction error, SST is summed squared deviation of observations from their mean, and n is count. A constant observed series has undefined explained-variation ratio.
Use a:b = (a/g):(b/g), where g = gcd(a,b) is the greatest common divisor of the entered nonnegative integers. The quantities cannot both be zero.
Use V = lwh/3 and S = lw+l√(h²+(w/2)²)+w√(h²+(l/2)²). l and w are rectangular base dimensions and h is perpendicular height, all in the same unit. S includes the base.
Use A = ns²/[4tan(π/n)] and P = ns. n is the number of equal sides and s is side length. The tangent uses radians. A is area and P is perimeter.
Use A = d₁d₂/2 and s = √(d₁²+d₂²)/2. d₁ and d₂ are the rhombus diagonals in the same length unit. A is area and s is side length.
Use RR = (a/n)/(b/m) and D = a/n−b/m. a and b are event counts for groups A and B; n and m are their totals. D is the probability difference, displayed in percentage points.
Use R = √[Σxᵢ²/n]. xᵢ are observations and n is their count. The root mean square R is nonnegative and uses the observations' unit.

Use R = sign(x)round(abs(x)×10^p)/10^p. x is the value and p is decimal places. abs means absolute value; sign restores the sign. Halfway cases round away from zero; negative places round to larger place values.

Use n₀ = (zσ/E)². σ is assumed population deviation, E is desired half-width, and z is the two-sided normal critical value. For finite population N, use n = n₀/[1+(n₀−1)/N]; otherwise keep the uncorrected value. Round up to a whole sample count.
Write x = m×10^e. x is the entered value, m is the coefficient, and e is an integer exponent. For nonzero input, 1 ≤ abs(m) < 10; abs means absolute value. Zero uses zero coefficient and exponent.
Convert the entered angle a in degrees to θ = πa/180 radians. Use A = r²θ/2 and s = rθ. r is radius, A is sector area, and s is arc length.
Use Cₑ = 1/Σ(1/Cᵢ). Each Cᵢ is a positive series capacitance in µF. Sum reciprocals and take the reciprocal again; equivalent capacitance Cₑ remains in µF.
Use Rₑ = ΣRᵢ. Each Rᵢ is a positive series resistor value in Ω. The equivalent resistance Rₑ uses the same unit; the sum covers every entered resistor.
Use H = −Σpᵢln(pᵢ) and J = H/ln(S). pᵢ is each positive category count divided by total count, and S is category count. ln is natural logarithm. A single category uses the convention J = 1.
Use H = −Σpᵢlog₂(pᵢ). pᵢ are probability fractions totaling unity. Zero-probability terms contribute zero. The logarithm base makes entropy H measured in bits.
Use m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) for points (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂). m is slope. The points must differ; equal horizontal coordinates produce a vertical line with undefined slope.

Use n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂. n₁ and n₂ are incident and transmitted refractive indices; θ₁ and θ₂ are angles from the normal. Angles are entered and displayed in degrees. If refraction has no real angle, the result identifies total internal reflection.
Use L = 10log₁₀(I/Iᵣ). I is sound intensity and Iᵣ is reference intensity in the same unit. Sound intensity level L is in dB.
Use r = √x with r ≥ 0. x is the nonnegative radicand and r is its principal square root. The other displayed root is its opposite.
Use SE = s/√n. s is sample standard deviation and n is the number of independent observations. Standard error describes variability of a sample mean, not the spread of individual observations.
Use P = kAΔT/L. k is conductivity in W/m·K, A is area in m², ΔT is the signed hot-minus-cold temperature difference in K, and L is thickness in m. Heat flow rate P is in W.
Use P = εσA(T⁴−Tₛ⁴). ε is emissivity, σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, A is area in m², and T and Tₛ are surface and surrounding temperatures in K. Positive P means net outward power in W.

Use 1/f = 1/dₒ+1/dᵢ and m = −dᵢ/dₒ. f is focal length, dₒ is object distance, and dᵢ is image distance in the same unit. A converging focal length and real object distance are positive; m is lateral magnification.
Use τ = rF sinθ. r is distance to the force application point in m, F is force magnitude in N, and θ is their included angle in degrees. Torque magnitude τ is in N·m.
Use A = (a+b)h/2 and m = (a+b)/2. a and b are parallel side lengths and h is perpendicular height in the same unit. m is midline length.

Use P = max(0,min(b,h)−max(a,l))/(b−a). a and b are continuous uniform distribution bounds, and l and h are query bounds. The formula measures the overlap divided by the distribution width; the result is displayed as a percentage.
Use M = √(x²+y²+z²) and u = (x/M,y/M,z/M). x, y and z are vector components, M is magnitude, and u is the unit direction. The vector must be nonzero.
Use Vₒ = VᵢR₂/(R₁+R₂). Vᵢ is input voltage, R₁ is the upper resistor, and R₂ is the lower resistor in the same resistance unit. Output Vₒ is measured across the lower resistor without a load.

Use t = (m₁−m₂)/√(s₁²/n₁+s₂²/n₂). m, s and n are each sample's mean, sample standard deviation and size; subscripts distinguish the samples. The two-sided p-value uses Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, without assuming equal variances.

Each side needs S = (T−B)/2. T is target total weight and B is bar weight in the same unit. Choose matching plate pairs to reach S on each side with the fewest plates. Each entered plate size is assumed to have enough matching pairs.

Compare L₁ = ceil(W/R)(L+t) and L₂ = ceil(L/R)(W+t), then choose the smaller requirement. L and W are room length and width, R is carpet roll width, and t is extra trim on each strip, all in m. ceil rounds the strip count up.

Use L = B⁻¹(α/2;k,n−k+1) and U = B⁻¹(1−α/2;k+1,n−k). k is successes and n is trials. For confidence-level fraction c, set α = 1−c; B⁻¹ is the beta quantile. Handle boundaries k = 0 → L = 0 and k = n → U = 1.
Use T₂ = T₁(D₂/D₁)^e. T₁ is known finish time, D₁ is known distance, D₂ is target distance in the same unit, and e is the editable endurance exponent. Projected time T₂ uses the original time unit.

For r = 0, cut length is c = h+t; for r > 0, use c = r ceil((h+t)/r). Rolls are N = ceil[ceil(P/w)/floor(L/c)]. h is wall height, t is trim, r is pattern repeat, P is wall perimeter, w is roll width, and L is roll length, all in m. ceil rounds up and floor rounds down.
Uses internal rectangular dimensions and a uniformly sloping floor. Steps, benches, curved walls and changes in water level are not modeled.
Estimates one rainfall event using entered collection efficiency and free tank capacity. Does not forecast rainfall or assess water quality and drinking safety.
Assumes constant total emitter flow and the entered application efficiency. The water-depth target is chosen by you; crop needs, soil behavior and weather are not assessed.
Uses the product seed rate and pack mass you enter, with an optional waste allowance. Does not choose a seed variety, sowing season or agronomic application rate.
Assumes constant annual consumption and electricity price. Payback includes energy savings only; maintenance, financing, resale and appliance lifetime are excluded.
Assumes the entered average moving speed and total stop time. Does not include live traffic, weather delays or route planning.
Transport and accommodation are group costs; daily spending is per person. Use one currency throughout. No exchange rates or live travel prices are supplied.
Preferment is treated as flour and water only. Water from eggs, milk and other ingredients is not included. Hydration compares total water mass with total flour mass.
Estimates collected water from one rainfall event using your collection efficiency and remaining tank space. Does not forecast rainfall or assess water quality and drinking safety.
Enter electricity drawn from the supply, including charging losses. Excludes maintenance, insurance, taxes, depreciation and incentives.

This release includes a pocket keypad, a scientific keypad, practical calculators across nine categories and three original planning scenarios. Language pages and embedded views are not counted as separate tools.
